issues.body: This issue outlines the recipe for our first end-to-end post-training run for Mochi.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖

# Research

#11191 does not yet identify a parent checkpoint, RL task/data, compute budget, or acceptance evaluations. The latest [#8089](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8089) update reports full-model Mochi SFT attempt 2 in progress, starting from step 393491 and targeting a permanent checkpoint at step 400407. The base checkpoint has a schema-3 export, but [#11127](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11127) still tracks the vLLM wheel/pin and serving–trainer checks needed for RL. The [Hero RL readiness record](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10388) establishes a 4K GSM8K learning and restore pilot on older revisions, not qualification of the post-SFT checkpoint or current stack.

# Plan

1. **Freeze the run contract.** Select the completed #8089 SFT checkpoint only after verifying its step, metadata, and export. Pin the Marin/SkyRL/vLLM revisions, tokenizer and chat template, RL data and held-out evaluation revisions, initial checkpoint, output root, W&B ID, resume/checkpoint policy, topology, cost ceiling, DRI, and stop criteria. Reuse the existing Marin post-training orchestration and SkyRL training path; publish the effective config and dry-run output before launch.
2. **Qualify the model handoff.** Finish the schema-3 vLLM wheel and Marin/SkyRL pins in #11127, export the selected SFT checkpoint, and check tokenizer/template/EOT behavior and fixed-weight serving–trainer agreement. Keep the first pilot at a 4,096-token combined cap; require the #11127 long-context parity checks before extending past 65,536 tokens.
3. **Run a bounded online pilot.** Start with the 4K GSM8K task and held-out panel used for prior Hero RL qualification in #10388, using a pinned dataset split and no training/eval overlap. Gate continuation on non-skipped optimizer updates, finite loss and routing metrics, rollouts from synchronized updated weights, checkpoint save/resume, and an independently loadable export. Recheck the earlier log-probability and clipping acceptance measurements on this exact checkpoint/runtime; the historical pass does not transfer automatically.
4. **Evaluate and decide.** Score the same held-out panel before and after RL, report paired differences and uncertainty, throughput/cost, failures, and exact artifact links. Expand to the selected multi-domain recipe only after the pilot and budget review; keep negative results in this issue. The run is complete when the final checkpoint/export, evaluation samples, run configuration, and reproducible run record are linked here.

Before launch, the owner needs to choose the first full-run RL task mixture and compute ceiling; the 4K GSM8K pilot above is the proposed qualification gate, not a substitute for those choices.

issues.title: Mochi e2e post-training run #1

issues.author: karansag
issues.body:
## TL;DR

Ablations on Snowball (the 10/05 SFT model) to choose SFT and RL settings for the Mochi 535B post-training run. Each experiment has a 1 h version and an 8 h version. Most backlog items have not run yet; current results are under Status.

## Description

Snowball is a smaller Grug MoE with the same post-training stack as Mochi. Each experiment changes one setting of the SFT or RL recipe (data, optimizer, loss mask, precision, tool format, RL task choice) and compares it against a matched control. The arms are read out with Micro210, BFCL ×5 and a retention panel. Experiments that look useful are then checked on Mochi.

Issue 11177 made the long loop runnable from the 10/05 SFT. Issue 11337 tracks run-ready Snowball recipes and Micro eval scores. Issue 11531 tracks Snowball long-loop SFT on TPU v4.

## Hypothesis or Goal

Find which recipe settings change Snowball's agentic and tool-use scores enough to carry into Mochi's next SFT/RL stage.

## Sub-issues

Each result is posted on its own issue:
- Snowball long-loop SFT on TPU v4: issue 11531
- Malformed JSON in nested Pi edit calls: issue 11536
- SFT optimizer, Muon-H vs Adam (C150 vs O150): issue 11537
- TMax data, with vs without: issue 11539
- RL samples per prompt: issue 11594
- Mochi BFCL ×5 versus Snowball models: issue 11538
- First expert-Muon-H train step stalls on 64 H100s: issue 11646
- Does teacher closeness predict SFT outcome: issue 11673
- Measured student NLL closeness to teacher traces: issue 11674
- Bug, long-loop SFT screens stored parameters in BF16 (FP32 comparison and affected runs): issue 11687
- Rolling recovery checkpoints and single final saves in long-loop SFT: issue 11714
- What Mochi is similar to (NLL and behaviour against open-weight models): issue 11722
- Mochi SFT (step 400407) weakness analysis and candidate target skills: issue 11723
- Teacher soft targets and temperature matching for Snowball SFT: issue 11724
- GPU train step ~3x slower in the process that compiled it than when loaded from the persistent compile cache: issue 11775
- Pretraining replay share (20%, 40%, and 60% from the pre-train base): issue 11783
- First SFT update hangs on 64 H100s with Adam expert banks and FP32: issue 11793
- Which Exp1-to-Exp4 SFT changes cost general and agentic ability: issue 11858
- Two-speed Snowball SFT on 64 H100 (45-55 s vs 120-128 s/update): issue 11909
- Add barrier_sync_named after rebind_first_state (10-min NCCL clique-ID timeout on host-rebind skew): issue 11944

## Status

- **Tool-call format:** in the FP32 from-base pair (one training run per arm), replacing 41 of 4,800 rows with synthetic Pi edit-call exercises scored 120 of 855 on the edit-call test (higher on 10 of 11 tasks) and Micro210 score mass 97.39 / 99.33 (mean 98.36 of 440), against 63 of 855 and 87.30 / 87.28 (mean 87.29) for the control; native equal-20 overlapped across repeats (20.21% vs 19.12%), AIME24 and OlympiadBench accounted for 11.00 of the 11.07 mass points (the other 18 sources netted +0.07, with tool-use sources not clearly improving), and both arms sat far below the 2026-11-18 from-base control (145.01) and 10/05 (175.75). Earlier 15-update FP32 continuations from 10/05 scored 284 to 293 of 855 against 224 for 10/05 (issue 11687), and a partial Mochi screen found far fewer broken edit calls (7 of 358 against Snowball's 524 of 1,093) but ended undecided. On a weak baseline (one run per arm), the edit-data run scored nearly twice as high on the edit-call test with no measured cost to general ability, so we keep the edit-call rows in the mix; the effect size on a healthy model and any gain on real agent tasks are not yet measured, and earlier BF16 runs through 2026-11-18 carried the BF16 stored-parameter caveat (issue 11687). See issue 11536.
- **SFT optimizer (Muon-H vs Adam):** the two evals disagree—BFCL favors Muon-H (30.2% against 24.6 to 24.7%), Micro210 favors Adam (41.9% against 37.7%), and training loss is about the same. No winner; we kept Muon-H because it matches pretraining and ran no more arms, and both runs had the BF16 stored-parameter precision bug (issue 11687), so this comparison should not be used to choose an optimizer. See issue 11537.
- **TMax pair:** the TMax run fits held-out TMax traces better (loss 0.299 against 0.587) but scores lower on BFCL (209/615 against 262/615 with the training template), and Micro210 is incomplete (two of the three runs failed). No clean answer: these runs stored weights in BF16 (issue 11687) and trained on whole traces rather than only assistant turns, so the question stays open until a redo with FP32 weights and assistant-only loss. See issue 11539.
- **Mochi BFCL ×5 (Pi agent, 123 tasks):** 450/615 (73.17%) record score under the configured retry rule; 449 first-attempt wins, one first-attempt reward unavailable after a timeout (bounding the first-attempt mean at 73.01–73.17%), against 33.98–52.36% for Snowball models. Because serving hardware and code revisions differed between the Mochi and Snowball runs, the comparison is descriptive; attributing the gap to the model alone would require a matched rerun. See issue 11538.

## Links

* Logbook:
* W&B Report:
* Important updates:

## Decision Log

- 2026-11-16: Flat edit tool ruled out for reported benchmarks and the default harness. The fix for malformed edits goes on the model side (SFT data).
- 2026-11-16: The SFT training data's tool calls were audited: 452 of 47.4M assistant call spans failed a JSON check. No data repair.

## Conclusion

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 The C150, O150 and TMax SFT arms have trained but still need Micro210 readouts. The E12 one-hour arms also await readout; [#11536](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11536) tracks their nested-edit hypothesis. The two published [long-loop recipes](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11337) changed training recipes and have different scoring coverage, so their aggregate scores do not isolate an ablation effect.

Plan:
1. For each SFT or RL setting, pin a control and one-setting treatment at the one-hour and eight-hour budgets. Match the starting checkpoint, source and data revisions outside the tested change, task IDs, seeds, Pi harness, and eval policy. Preserve the consumed configs and checkpoint revisions.
2. Finish the pending C150/O150/TMax and E12 one-hour Micro210 readouts first. Compare matching task IDs and report scored/unscored counts, per-benchmark and aggregate deltas, BFCL ×5, and the retention panel. Include malformed nested-edit rates for E12. Use [#11536's gate](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11536): at least a 50% rate reduction against its control with no Micro210 or retention loss.
3. Advance arms with a positive paired agentic/tool-use result and no retention regression to matched eight-hour controls. Repeat the same panels, report uncertainty and incomplete coverage, and record null or adverse results. Check surviving settings on Mochi before selecting its SFT/RL recipe.
4. Keep an arm table here with the changed setting, control and treatment pins, both budget readouts, BFCL and retention results, and the carry/drop decision. Add each run-ready recipe, exact data mix, Micro policy, immutable checkpoint, and archive receipts to [#11337](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11337).

## Metric definitions

Equal-20 is recomputed from the 20 native per-source avg_score fields. Those fields include excluded assignments in their denominators. Available-only columns omit excluded scores and therefore use different denominators.

Task-equivalent differences are n × (arm mean − parent run 1 mean), summed over sources. Here n counts assignments, not necessarily distinct task identities. Fractional graders produce fractional task-equivalents, not additional integer wins. No individual task outcomes have been paired.

BFCL /10 is the native score mass for the ten-assignment Micro slice. C150 has five known score units, nine scored assignments and one unknown outcome: its assigned score bounds are 5–6 /10. The regional parent has seven known score units over nine scored assignments plus one unknown: assigned bounds 7–8 /10. This slice is not the earlier 123-task ×5 BFCL evaluation.

The parent repeat has seven unknown outcomes: one BixBench and six TB2. The first parent reports 440/440 scored and zero excluded. Both have complete native aggregate dumps; the repeat does not have complete scored outcomes. The two runs use the same configured seed and recipe, not independent training seeds or proven matched random streams.

## Evidence boundaries

All 14 scored rows have reviewed native aggregates and terminal resource accounting. For the earlier seven rows, individual source files were metadata-listed, not independently checked for exact assigned-UID membership, raw exceptions or file hashes. Each current TMax and cw-rno2a dump has 21 streamed and hashed files, 440 unique expected UID strings, and all 20 source means/counts/exclusions reconciled under the frozen UID-source mapping. That reduced extraction does not independently prove the actual source-file-to-UID/task join. Produced suite artifacts match the 440-row reference bytes and order where checked; that does not attest live runtime consumption. Native completion, archive membership and trace capture are separate evidence.

Requested H100-hours are physical-attempt resource envelopes, not utilization, invoices or Pod/provider-release timing. Native success is not broad-suite green or evidence that the unresolved import failures are harmless.

The two parent judge workers and brokers each had only A0. Their final preemption_count of one accompanies terminal KILLED cleanup after the policy child finished; no native restart gap was found. This does not prove continuous HTTP health or explain the repeat's seven exclusions. The bound vllm_server.py is identical between those runs; a different file in the current checkout is not a run-to-run source change or a deployed-byte readback.

It reported 438/440 scored, two excluded, native equal-20 45.065889%, available equal-20 45.101604% and pooled available 38.591730%. The old TMax arm failed and yielded a conservative recovered subset of 437/440: available macro 52.39%, pooled 44.99%, three unknown. There was no complete native aggregate for that arm. Neither result fills a current-harness row. The superseded failed parent recovery is not used here.

The two current TMax runs bind the original cw-us-east-02a exports without copying: arm 134,181,708,393 B; control 134,181,708,404 B. Both have 87 HF objects and 39 weight shards. Fresh metadata and header checks are not a new full tensor-payload parity audit.

Both current roots and policy children succeeded, each with seven terminal jobs and seven A0 attempts. The arm has one BixBench exclusion; control has one TB2 exclusion. Both remain unknown. Available-only weighting changes BixBench 1/10 to 1/9 in the arm and TB2 2/30 to 2/29 in control. Their task-difference bounds refer to these unknown scores, not confidence intervals or matched task outcomes.

The same startup config-parse diagnostic appeared in both completed parent logs and TMax; later scoring superseded the early zero-ready snapshot. Its cause and harmlessness are not established. Terminal accounting does not establish both GPU Pods absent or provider release.

## RL training, exports and native closure

Both RL training arms reached saved step-10 native checkpoints, but their training roots failed during teardown. Both HF exports are structurally verified in cw-rno2a. The two Micro210 repetitions per export and regional parent all have successful roots and policies, seven terminal jobs and seven observed A0 attempts per evaluation. Judge workers and brokers were KILLED after policy completion. No retry or continuous-health inference follows from the one-attempt observations. W&B in-run metrics and teacher-closeness NLL are not Micro210.

Accepted failure/preemption/job-wide retry limits are explicit: root 0/0/0; policy 0/1000/0; judge 1/10/1; broker 0/1000/0; prepare-model 1/100/0; prepare_micro and verify_ready_inputs each 0/100/0. Limits are not counts of observed retries. Timeout waits are per wait, not total-completion guarantees; native TIMEOUT bypasses ordinary requeue.

All 39 same-named shard hashes recorded in the two export manifests differ between the RL exports and from the parent's retained verified shard hashes. The two RL exports have identical byte totals and index layout; that does not make them the same model. The harness selects the separately pinned tools tokenizer and template, not the export's embedded template. Contributor SFT is not run and the full run is not planned. Only a two-update smoke existed. Both current TMax rows and all five cw-rno2a rows have reviewed native aggregates and terminal resource accounting. No causal optimizer/SFT/RL finding, calibrated significance or equivalence claim follows from this table.

🤖 ## Finding: the long-loop SFT ablations used a different optimizer grouping from 10/05 and Mochi

Found on 2026-11-17 while preparing an arm that restores the 10/05 optimizer state: the saved state did not fit the optimizer that the long-loop SFT code builds.

## What differs

| Parameter family | 10/05 (saved optimizer state, logged config) | Mochi SFT (sealed source, hero-EP optimizer) | Long-loop SFT ablations (bound source) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Stacked expert `w_gate` / `w_up` / `w_down` (4-D) | MuonH | MuonH | **Adam** |
| Stacked `rms_attn` / `rms_mlp` scales (2-D) | Adam | Adam | **MuonH** |
| Shared expert weights (3-D) | MuonH | MuonH | MuonH |
| Gradient clipping | none | not compared | **1.0** (E12 config) |

## Cause

The long-loop `sft.py` imports the generic `experiments/grug/moe/optimizer.py`. Its MuonH rule accepts only 2-D and 3-D weights and has no rule that sends RMSNorm scales to Adam. With stacked blocks the 4-D expert weights fall through to Adam and the 2-D stacked norm scales go to MuonH. The June TPU optimizer implementation that the 10/05 model card links to, which is consistent with that run's saved optimizer slots and logged config, and the hero-EP optimizer in the sealed Mochi source both handle the stacked case explicitly (RMSNorm scales to Adam, 2-D to 4-D weights to MuonH). The generic file at `main` commit `18ae01ee42` is byte-identical to the one the ablations used.

## Runs affected

- **Affected (bound source and published consumed configs; worker import bytes not separately attested):** the E12 all-weights and general-only arms, the TMax arm and its control, C150, and the low-learning-rate replay rerun of 2026-11-17.
- **Related code, swapped families not trained:** the E12 attention-and-head-only arm freezes the expert and norm families, so the swap does not act on it.
- **Not affected:** Mochi SFT through step 400,407 (from its sealed source, not a fresh worker attestation); O150 (plain Adam by design); the RL arms (Megatron AdamW).

## What this does and does not show

- The E12 all-weights and general-only arms and the TMax arm and control used this grouping in their bound source. None is a matched test of the 10/05 optimizer set-up.
- It is a candidate cause of that drop. It is **not** shown to be the cause; no run with the corrected grouping has been evaluated yet.
- The 10/05 grouping is established from its logged optimizer config (`rmsnorm_to_adam=true`, no clipping) and its saved optimizer slots. The exact commit that run was launched from is not recorded in its W&B run.

## Next

1. A replay-only arm on 10/05 (15 updates, fresh optimizer state, learning rate 5e-6) with the 10/05 grouping and no clipping. The grouping change labels all 27 parameter leaves of the model the same way as the 10/05 optimizer state.
2. The same arm with the uncorrected grouping finished training on 2026-11-17 and is being evaluated; the pair gives the comparison.
3. A fix for the generic optimizer, or a switch of the long-loop SFT code to the hero-EP optimizer, follows as a PR.

comments.body:
🤖 Status, November 19 (UTC).

## Plan change

The Mochi plan is one big SFT and one big RL. After an independent review of the ablation plan, we stopped every run that continues SFT from 10/05. Ablations now start from the pre-train base, change one thing per arm, and compare against a base-start control. Added traces train on assistant turns only.

## Today's updates

| Issue | What changed |
|---|---|
| [SFT runs, issue 11687](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11687#issuecomment-7016318555) | Eight-hour pair: no measurable held-out loss difference. Runs from 10/05 cancelled. Base-start control running; Run A (edit-call data) and Run B (TMax traces) next. |
| [RL group size, issue 11594](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11594#issuecomment-7016135637) | Step-20 results for 4 and 8 rollouts per prompt |
| [Slow updates, issue 11646](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11646#issuecomment-7015968717) | Cause found: runs that compile in-process are about 2.7x slower; a short compile job first avoids it |
| [Mochi similarity, issue 11722](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11722#issuecomment-7015832530) | Nemotron v3 is 80.6% of the SFT mix; similarity work stops here |
| [Mochi weaknesses, issue 11723](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11723#issuecomment-7016319485) | Skill A awaits its `mrcr-65k` score; Skill B Mochi run parked |

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
August 20th: noticed that we are OOMing every ~3 hours.

We attempted interventions to adjust XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_MEM_FRACTION=0.83 (giving XLA more memory). This made things worse. 

--xla_gpu_memory_limit_slop_factor seems to be another promising tunable. Adjusting to 0.88 from the default 0.95 didn't help. Testing with 0.85 now.

In theory fraction 0.83 with slop 88 strictly dominates the baseline, as a followup to test if the lowered thresholds don't hold.

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
We observed periodic host OOMs after several checkpoints. https://echo.oa.dev/wiki/200 . Restarting with the following changes:

1. Tensorstore restore parallelism bounded by a fixed budget
2. Checkpoint offload cache to 16GB
3. malloc_trim() calls after each checkpoint

in theory 2 will make checkpoints faster (fully async), and 3 will prevent the host OOM recurrence

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
`malloc_trim` was still inconsistently resulting in OOMs during checkpointing. Restarting on main with the jemalloc changes in.

Restores were hitting single worker stalls. Merged and running with #8584 . First restore after this change was successful, though it might have been luck/caching.

comments.body: 🤖 Correction after tracing the current checkpoint path: the long-lived `GlobalAsyncCheckpointManager` keeps the completed TensorStore commit futures in `_commit_futures`; `wait_until_finished()` joins but does not clear them, and the writes allow indefinite source-buffer references. PR #8599 contained a reviewed post-join cleanup for these futures, but that part did not land with #8609. comments.author: mcwitt-agent
comments.body:
🤖 Storage incident on 2026-09-23/24, now resolved. At 23:44Z the US-EAST-08A CoreWeave account reached 104.56 TiB against its 100 TiB quota, and CoreWeave suspended writes (`405 MethodNotAllowed: Account is write suspended for this availability zone`). Most of the 11.7 TiB rise since 20:26Z came from this deploy's forced checkpoints and durable handoff copies in `hero-checkpoints`.

- The step-146585 save staged at 23:43:47Z and hung: rank 0 blocked in the s3fs manifest upload, which has no timeout. Training and logs stopped with no error. The step watchdog restarted the gang at about 00:00Z (attempt 1), which restored `step-146355`.
- Russell's cleanup brought usage to about 80 TB by 00:21Z. Writes were accepted again from 00:39Z.
- Attempt 1's step-146582 save at 01:01Z then stalled. 448 of 704 processes finished their upload; the other 256, spread over 132 hosts, stopped writing at 01:01:55Z with no error, and the commit never completed. Host memory stayed about 260 GiB below the limit. The cause is not confirmed; a storage-side stall left over from the suspension is the leading explanation. Training continued because checkpoint uploads run in background threads, but the next save would have blocked on it, so the task was preempted at 01:40Z (attempt 2, again from `step-146355`).
- Since then, saves `step-146582` (02:43Z) and `step-146817` (03:44Z) committed normally, and the first evaluation at step 147000 matched the trend: dropless loss 1.9086 against 1.9098 at step 144000.
- Cost: steps 146355–146732 were trained twice, plus about two hours of hangs and restarts.
- Cleanup: about 49 TB of stale temporary checkpoints and duplicates were deleted from `hero-checkpoints`. The durable handoff copies for steps 108778, 121638, and 146139 remain. The step-81716 handoff was deleted during the incident cleanup, and no durable copy of the step-58014 handoff was found.

🤖 October 3 hero stall, read-only triage: attempt 12 reached step 197999, then task 120 local rank 3 (global 483) failed the step-198000 save at 10:06:33 UTC. The other 703 ranks timed out at `tensorstore_checkpoint_17::0`, and Iris requeued the 176-task gang.

Attempt 13 selected complete checkpoint step 197637. At 11:24 UTC, all 176 trainer pods were Running but training had not resumed. NCCL reported all 704 ranks present; ranks 68–71 (task 17) were the only AllReduce progress outliers. Two native profiles show all four task-17 ranks stuck in XLA `backend_compile_and_load` before checkpoint loading, while sampled peers wait in restore AllReduce. Task 17 is on `s2brxs64`; its LOTA proxy logged upstream TCP timeouts and HTTP 502 for `hero-checkpoints` at 10:09–10:11. Task-17 ranks also logged cache-read 502 errors. Direct node boot and condition reads were denied, so recurrence of the October 2 node fault is unverified.

The run has lost at least 78 minutes since the failed save and would replay steps 197638–197999 from the selected checkpoint. Next: have a node-read-authorized operator verify `s2brxs64` boot/health and storage connectivity, escalate the 400/502 evidence to CoreWeave storage support, then have the production owner decide on targeted recovery. No infrastructure or job mutation was made.

Epic for the [First rounds of post-training Mochi (SFT+RLVR)](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/milestone/15) milestone (due December 21).

**Goal:** RL (RLVR) runs on Mochi and Snowball that start reliably, keep the GB200 racks busy, and survive the faults we have already seen, so that #11191 can run more than a handful of updates.

**Already in flight**
- #11120 consolidated Snowball and Mochi long-loop RL (PR)
- #11954 Mochi decode-throughput sprint (closed; fix plan awaiting review before relaunch)
- #11969 Snowball RL resizing sprint
- #11957 one explicit rollout concurrency budget
- #11127 export, serve and RL-train the log-scaled hero
- #11948 enforce NVLink-domain exclusions in Iris
- #11649 NCCL corruption at 32 ranks (fixed by #11838; upstream NVIDIA/nccl#2625)

Recipe choice lives in #11535; the end-to-end run in #11191.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖

# Research

#12003 spans rollout throughput, launch placement, serving compatibility, and recovery. #11954 measured a 2.169× per-GPU rollout-rate gain for the selected Mochi geometry, but the `.120` training run ended after its first update; its Track 1 fixes await coordinator review before relaunch. #11969 is still sizing Snowball: its first H100 4-worker measurement spent 588.0 of 687.6 seconds (85.5%) waiting for rollouts. Existing work covers the long loop (#11120), NVLink exclusions (#11948), concurrency limits (#11957), log-scaled serving (#11127), and the 32-rank NCCL fault (#11649, fixed by #11838).

# Plan

1. Review #11954's Track 1 receipt and serving-cap probe with the coordinator before any Mochi RL relaunch. Pin the consumed round YAML, runtime, vLLM wheel, log-scaled export, and NCCL setting; run a bounded startup, evaluation, checkpoint, and recovery gate on that exact source.
2. Finish #11969's Snowball worker/engine sizing ladder. Compare clean-update time, rollout-wait fraction, generated tokens per GPU-second, and GPU-hours per update against the current layout; publish the consumed configs and run receipts.
3. Settle #11120's shared-loop landing path and the open #11948/#11957 dependencies through their existing issues and PRs. Verify NVLink placement, the binding concurrency limit, weight/replica checks, and checkpoint restore before a sustained run.
4. Freeze the SFT/RL recipe in #11535, then run #11191 on the selected layouts. Close this epic after both Snowball and Mochi exceed the previous 17-update Snowball failure with at least 20 committed RL updates, recover from a worker or process failure, retain selected/final checkpoints, and report evaluation coverage, GPU utilization, update time, and GPU-hours per update.

spillover_issues.body:
Four generated Reasoning Gym tasks give full reward to a reply that does not depend on the question. `reasoning_gym_generated` holds 1,000 rows of each.

- `game_of_life_halting`: every non-blank reply scores 1.0 on all 1,000 entries. The scorer compares `bool(reply)` with `bool(answer)`, and every answer is the string `True` or `False`. [The generator](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/d83e7766c5a5b9bec43cdd26eccc71a54dcf9bfd/experiments/post_training/task_curation/datasets/reasoning_gym/generate.py#L77-L86) records the reward of the fixed wrong answer `definitely wrong` for every row. For these 1,000 rows the recorded reward is 1.0, and [`convert_generated`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/d83e7766c5a5b9bec43cdd26eccc71a54dcf9bfd/experiments/post_training/task_curation/datasets/reasoning_gym/tasks.py#L256-L271) stores the record without reading it.
- `complex_arithmetic`: the reply `NaN` scores 1.0 on all 1,000 entries. The scorer returns `min(1.0, math.exp(-distance))`, which is 1.0 when the distance is NaN.
- `coin_flip`: the reply `0` scores 1.0 on 939 of the 1,000 entries. The scorer of `reasoning-gym` 0.1.25 gives partial reward for a matching prefix and divides by the length of the shorter string, so the one-character reply `0` matches every answer that starts with `0.`.
- `propositional_logic`: the reply `P ∨ Q` scores 1.0 on 820 of the 1,000 entries. The scorer accepts any conclusion that follows from the premises, and a disjunction that names a premise follows from it.

Reproduce:

1. From the repository root, run:

   ```bash
   PYTHONHASHSEED=0 uv run --package marin-verifyit --extra reasoning-gym python - <<'EOF'
   import sys

   sys.path.insert(0, "experiments/post_training/task_curation/datasets/reasoning_gym")
   import generate
   import reasoning_gym

   replies = (
       ("game_of_life_halting", "x"),
       ("complex_arithmetic", "NaN"),
       ("coin_flip", "0"),
       ("propositional_logic", "P ∨ Q"),
   )
   for task, reply in replies:
       data = reasoning_gym.create_dataset(task, size=generate.ROWS_PER_TASK, seed=generate.task_seed(task))
       score = reasoning_gym.get_score_answer_fn(task)
       print(task, repr(reply), sum(score(reply, data[index]) == 1.0 for index in range(generate.ROWS_PER_TASK)))
   EOF
   ```

2. It prints `game_of_life_halting 'x' 1000`, `complex_arithmetic 'NaN' 1000`, `coin_flip '0' 939` and `propositional_logic 'P ∨ Q' 820`.

Expected: a constant reply does not earn full reward.

The recorded wrong answer scores 0 on `complex_arithmetic` and `coin_flip` and 0.05 or 0.25 on `propositional_logic`, so that record shows only the first of the four. Two of the four are in the Nemotron blend's part of the released validation panel (`open-athena/Snowball-Smartie-RL-2026.10.15.32-Data`): with the panel's own grade script, `P ∨ Q` scores 1.0 on six of its seven `propositional_logic` tasks and `NaN` on its one `complex_arithmetic` task.

I tried 44 constant replies on the first 100 entries of every generated task. No fifth task gives the full reward on more than a quarter of the entries to a constant that is not the entry's answer.

🤖 A fifth task belongs on this list: `puzzle24`. The reply `1*2*3*4` scores 1.0 on all 1,000 of its generated entries. The scorer of `reasoning-gym` 0.1.25 (`reasoning_gym/games/puzzle24.py` L114-L132) checks that the reply evaluates to 24 and contains four numbers between 1 and 10. It does not read the entry's numbers. Five of the 1,000 entries have the numbers 1, 2, 3 and 4. The recorded wrong answer `definitely wrong` scores 0.01 on every entry, so that record does not show it.

The last paragraph of the issue says that no fifth task pays a constant on more than a quarter of its entries. None of the 44 constants I tried evaluates to 24, so that sweep could not find this task.

To check, add `("puzzle24", "1*2*3*4")` to `replies` in the script above. It prints `puzzle24 '1*2*3*4' 1000`. `puzzle24` is not in the released validation panel.

🤖 After #11987, `propositional_logic` still pays a reply that ignores the question, and it pays most correct conclusions 0. The task asks for "a correct conclusion", and the merged scorer compares the reply's text with the entry's `example_answer`, which is one of many valid conclusions. On the 1,000 generated entries (reasoning-gym 0.1.25, the generator's seeds), with the scorer on main `18a6cd646`:

- The 1,000 entries have 61 distinct examples. `(P ∨ Q)` is the example on 73 of them, so the constant reply `(P ∨ Q)` scores 1.0 on 73.
- Restating one of the entry's premises as the conclusion scores 1.0 for 81 of the 2,998 premises. The pinned scorer gave 1.0 to the 1,759 that are not trivial.
- Comparing with the example by truth table, as the review on #11987 suggested, would raise the constant `(P ∨ Q)` to 132 entries. 344 of the 2,998 premises are equivalent to their entry's example.

So comparing with the recorded example does not measure inference here, and the pinned scorer's rule (any entailed formula that is not trivial) admits the weakening `P ∨ Q`. I don't see a per-entry rule that rejects that weakening and still accepts the generator's own examples, because many examples are weakenings themselves: seed 42's first entry has the premises `R` and `Q` and the example `(P ∨ Q)`. Leaving the family out of training and the validation panel until the task asks for a specific conclusion looks cleanest to me. @penfever, would you rather keep the rows and accept that, or have me send a PR that excludes the family?

The coin_flip tolerance from the same review is in #12006.

spillover_issues.body:
On Kubernetes, an unprivileged `bwrap` in a `CONTAINER_PROFILE_DEFAULT` task fails at its first mount:

```
bwrap: Failed to make / slave: Permission denied
```

Seen on cw-us-east-02a on 2026-10-26, with `bwrap --unshare-all --share-net --ro-bind /usr /usr ...` run as a non-root user (uid 1000) in the default task image. bwrap creates the user namespace, and the next mount fails with `EACCES`. That matches the container runtime's default AppArmor profile, which denies `mount`. A seccomp or capability denial returns `EPERM`.

`_security_context` sets no `appArmorProfile` for DEFAULT ([tasks.py#L785-L815](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/8577d258214dd0dcb992c04458ee4eb10496d4e5/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/backends/k8s/tasks.py#L785-L815)). Only PRIVILEGED removes AppArmor confinement, and it is host-root-equivalent and needs the admin role. [shellbox's README](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/8577d258214dd0dcb992c04458ee4eb10496d4e5/lib/shellbox/README.md) lists the same requirement for bwrap.

So a job cannot put untrusted processes in a bubblewrap box (with their own PID, mount and UTS namespaces) unless its outer container is privileged.

Done when:
- A profile that is not elevated sets `appArmorProfile: {type: Unconfined}`. It keeps DEFAULT's capabilities, seccomp behavior and egress policies.
- A non-root `bwrap --unshare-all --share-net --ro-bind /usr /usr ... true` succeeds in a task with that profile on cw-us-east-02a.
- `lib/iris/docs/container-profiles.md` describes the profile and what it permits.

Kubernetes `DEFAULT` adds `SYS_PTRACE` but leaves AppArmor at the runtime default; that profile denies bubblewrap's first mount after it enters a user namespace. Iris has no profile that changes AppArmor without granting host-root-equivalent `PRIVILEGED` access. The newer `SANDBOX` profile runs the outer task in gVisor, so it does not provide an inner bubblewrap environment for a GPU task.

**Relevant code**
- [`tasks.py#L790-L819`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/8577d258214dd0dcb992c04458ee4eb10496d4e5/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/backends/k8s/tasks.py#L790-L819) — Kubernetes security contexts

The independent Shellbox job `bubblewrap-10692-shellbox-20261122` used the same profile and attempted `LocalMachineFactory()` followed by a shell command that writes and reads `/app/probe`. Factory construction failed with `SandboxUnavailable`: both the bundled binary and `/usr/bin/bwrap` reported `bwrap: loopback: Failed RTM_NEWADDR: Operation not permitted`. comments.author: penfever
comments.body:
🤖 **Root cause of the failed live check: a host kernel restriction, not the pod profile.**

The diagnostic ran on cw-us-east-02a under CONTAINER_PROFILE_BUBBLEWRAP as uid/gid 65534. The evidence is on #11998 (comment 7089553707).

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| Seccomp | 0 (ruled out) |
| Pod AppArmor label | unconfined |
| `kernel.unprivileged_userns_clone` | 1 |
| `kernel.apparmor_restrict_unprivileged_userns` | **1** |
| Kernel | 6.8 (CoreWeave build) |
| `newuidmap` / `newgidmap` | absent |
| `unshare -Un true` | succeeds |
| `unshare -U --map-root-user` | uid_map write fails with EPERM |
| `bwrap --unshare-user` | uid_map write fails with EACCES |

With `apparmor_restrict_unprivileged_userns=1`, the kernel denies capabilities inside a new user namespace unless the creating process runs under an AppArmor profile that grants `userns`. A pod labelled `unconfined` does not get that grant. This also explains the earlier shellbox failure: setting up loopback (`RTM_NEWADDR`) needs `CAP_NET_ADMIN` inside the namespace.

**The fix is on the nodes. Either option needs approval before anyone applies it.**
1. Load an AppArmor profile on the CoreWeave worker nodes that allows `userns`, for example a profile with `userns,` and the rules bwrap needs. Set `appArmorProfile: {type: Localhost, localhostProfile: <name>}` for CONTAINER_PROFILE_BUBBLEWRAP instead of `Unconfined`. This keeps the restriction everywhere else.
2. Set `kernel.apparmor_restrict_unprivileged_userns=0` on the nodes. This is simpler but weaker, because it lifts the restriction for every pod on the node.

Option 1 is preferred. Whichever is chosen must be applied through the node and Pulumi management path, not by hand. The cw-us-east-02a controller has been returned to a clean `main` deployment while this is decided, and #11998 stays unmerged.

spillover_issues.author: penfever
spillover_issues.body:
Atlas ingest and RL each pick one task backend per task through fixed routes, and every backend requires an exact `command_semantics` match (`lib/shellbox/src/shellbox/machine.py:207`). A task's semantics label therefore acts as a rule rather than a hint. Forge's Daytona-only environment check refused its 352 `shell_simulator` task machines, and the refusal was then reported as "needs an unsupported backend", although production RL registers ShellSim in-process (`vendor/skyrl/marinskyrl/task_machine_factories.py:18`).

Task specs already declare their requirements: semantics, capabilities (`shell`, `filesystem`, `python`, `process`, `network`, `git_repository`), network policy, and an image or package source. Derive the backend from those requirements:

1. Declare one ordered tier table, cheapest first: ShellSim (in-process), local bubblewrap (package lock or prepared OCI filesystem), gVisor on Iris, Daytona (shared quota). Each tier lists the semantics, capabilities and sources it satisfies.
2. A `shell_simulator` task may run on a `linux_process` tier, because its capabilities are a subset of Linux's. A `linux_process` task never runs on ShellSim.
3. Ingest runs the task's oracle and negative controls on the cheapest available tier that satisfies its requirements. If the controls fail there, it retries on the next satisfying tier. It records the first tier where both controls pass as the task's route. A failure on the top satisfying tier is the task's final verdict.
4. RL routes each task to its recorded tier, replacing `task_machine_by_command_semantics`.

Done when:
- The tier table is the single place that maps requirements to backends, and Atlas ingest and RL both read it.
- Each admitted task records its route tier and the control verdicts of every tier it tried.
- A refusal from a backend check counts as "tier does not satisfy", never as "unsupported backend". A task is unsupported only when no tier that RL registers satisfies it.
- Forge's 352 ShellSim tasks are routed and verified through this path as the first cohort.

comments.author: penfever
comments.body:
🤖 Scope addition: the requirement fields are optional, so routing must handle specs that omit them.

`EnvironmentRequirements` defaults `capabilities` to `()` and `command_semantics` to `None` (`lib/taskcompendium/src/taskcompendium/models.py:360-361`). Harbor import declares `linux_process` and a pinned image, and its capabilities default to empty (`vendor/skyrl/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/dataset/harbor_import.py:124-143`). For these specs, an empty field means "not stated", not "needs nothing".

1. Inventory first: for each Atlas source, count specs that declare semantics, capabilities, network policy, and a source (image, lock, package spec). Post the table here before any routing change.
2. Conservative default: a spec with missing fields routes as it does today, to the tier its declared source requires, with the full Linux capability set assumed. This keeps current behavior and saves nothing.
3. Requirement analysis: a separate pass adds the missing fields to a source's specs, for example by reading verifier and solution scripts and the image's installed packages. Each added field is written to the spec with its evidence. Fail-up controls then confirm the cheaper route.

Done when also includes: the field inventory for every Atlas source, and analysis results for at least one source that currently omits capabilities.

🤖
# Research

[CampaignMachines](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/cd0e932c780e0171c5612658faa0f180a851569e/experiments/post_training/task_curation/pipeline.py#L271-L330) selects one factory from semantics or source, while [Shellbox](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/cd0e932c780e0171c5612658faa0f180a851569e/lib/shellbox/src/shellbox/machine.py#L194-L215) requires an exact semantics match. Ingest runs a golden *or* negative control, and its sampled verifier records a factory refusal as `UNSUPPORTED`; neither path can qualify a fallback tier. The final curation view drops control results, and the pending [SkyRL consumer](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11851) selects a backend from task or dataset configuration.

**Relevant code**
- [`controls.py#L143-L184`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/cd0e932c780e0171c5612658faa0f180a851569e/lib/taskcompendium/src/taskcompendium/pipeline/controls.py#L143-L184) — selects one control
- [`source_verification.py#L324-L365`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/cd0e932c780e0171c5612658faa0f180a851569e/lib/taskcompendium/src/taskcompendium/pipeline/source_verification.py#L324-L365) — sampled trial and refusal handling
- [`source_processing.py#L703-L719`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/cd0e932c780e0171c5612658faa0f180a851569e/lib/taskcompendium/src/taskcompendium/pipeline/source_processing.py#L703-L719) — final export columns

# Proposed Fix

This spans Shellbox, TaskCompendium, and SkyRL. [#11910](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11910) and [#11946](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11946) are changing LOCAL preparation and registration on top of #11851; build on those interfaces without a parallel implementation of their work.

1. Define one ordered, versioned tier table in Shellbox: ShellSim, local bubblewrap, gVisor on Iris, Daytona. Each entry declares accepted semantics, capability set, network policy, and materializable sources. Match `shell_simulator` on Linux tiers when its requirements fit; keep `linux_process` off ShellSim. Intersect matches with factories actually registered for RL.
2. Add per-task route qualification after normalization. Run both declared oracle and negative controls on the cheapest matching tier, retaining each tier's check results and refusal reason. Try the next matching tier after a control failure or backend refusal; keep infrastructure errors inconclusive under the existing retry policy. A failure on the highest matching tier is final. Tasks missing the required controls remain unverified; only zero RL-registered matching tiers is unsupported.
3. Store the selected tier, tier-table revision, and every attempted tier's verdict with each admitted task in curation metadata and the final export. Keep this execution evidence separate from the semantic `TaskSpec` JSON. Require a verified route for machine tasks even when source-level sampling passes.
4. Make SkyRL load that recorded tier, validate it against its registered factory, and stop selecting the actor through `task_machine_by_command_semantics`, dataset defaults, or the pending `required_backend` shortcut. Add matching, fallback, refusal, persistence, and consumer tests. Requalify all 352 Forge ShellSim tasks and publish counts and per-task route/control evidence before closing this issue.

🤖 Deliverable 0 — per-source inventory of declared task-requirement fields (scope addition, comment 7077980601)

**Method.** Every Atlas catalog source (413 on this branch, `experiments/post_training/task_curation/sources.py`) falls into exactly one task-construction path; the table groups sources by that path. comments.author: penfever
comments.body:
🤖 Requirement backfill: pricing and workflow design (scope addition 2)

**Population that actually needs backfilling.** Of the 1,580,750 tasks that declare `linux_process` semantics, 1,560,750 omit `capabilities` (Harbor archives 1,506,908 + rebuilt cohorts 53,842; the 20,000 shell-workspace rows already declare them), and no spec anywhere declares a network policy. Machine-less cohorts (2,978 forge rows + the RLVR conversations) have no task machine to describe, and the 283,520 agent-blend rows never route to shellbox — both out of scope. So the target is capabilities (and optionally network) on ~1.56M image tasks whose semantics and source are already declared; Forge's 606 admitted rows are already fully declared and its 352 archived `shell_simulator` rows route fine without backfill.

## Pricing per option

Assumptions: GLM-5.3 through the relay `/muchanem/glm53-relay` at 64 concurrent requests (the review pipeline's anchor); ~3–8k input + ~200–400 output tokens per task for an LLM proposal; Daytona sandbox cost estimated at $0.5–2/machine-hour — relay and Daytona accounting are internal, so dollar figures are estimates; token and machine-hour figures are the real quantities. Under-declaration is safe by design (the conservative default keeps today's route), so accuracy is discussed per direction of error.

| Option | Method | Evidence recorded | Accuracy | Cost per 1k | Cost for 1.58M | Wall time per 1k | Wall time for 1.58M | Failure modes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| (a) Static inference | Deterministic rules over the task's own bytes: grader/verifier and solution scripts, `task.toml`, Dockerfile lowering (the archived payloads carry them); image inspection cached per pinned base (~15 bases cover the Harbor archives) | Rule id + matched file path + sha256 per declared field | Semantics: verify-only (declared). Capabilities: high precision on explicit usage (curl/git/pytest/process), unknown recall for implicit needs. Under-declaration safe; over-declaration possible on loose regexes | ~0.06–0.3 vCPU-hour ≈ $0.02 | 88–440 vCPU-hours ≈ $5–30 compute | ~2 s (32-way) | 1.5–8 h on ~32 workers | Misses implicit needs (network via stdlib/subprocess, git via frameworks); cannot prove absence; rule drift needs the FP/FN ledger |
| (b) LLM-assisted proposal + control confirmation | One structured GLM-5.3 completion per task with the script and inventory in context; taskforge-style structural checks gate the proposal; tier ladder + controls confirm the route | LLM call-ledger record (taskforge `CallLedger`), quoted spans (checked against resource bytes), sampled control verdicts | Better recall on implicit needs; still cannot prove minimality; controls confirm sufficiency of the routed tier only for sampled tasks | ~4–8M in + 0.3M out tokens ≈ $2.4–5.4 | $3.9–8.7k API-side (+ probe cost if every task is confirmed) | ~15–30 s/task → 6–10 min at 64-way | ~5.5 days at 64-way (2–3 days batched) | Over-declaration (wrongly forces ALLOW or excludes a tier — the costly direction); hallucinated quotes (mitigated by byte-checking); prompt drift; cost |
| (c) Empirical probing (controls fail up) | Run the task's controls on the cheapest satisfying tier and fail up (the ladder landed in milestone 2); per-tier verdicts are the evidence | Executed per-tier verdicts, persisted on verification trials — the strongest evidence kind | Proves the tier suffices for what the control exercises; proves nothing about capabilities the control never touches (an empty control exercises almost nothing) | Local probe 1.4–5.6 vCPU-hours ≈ <$0.5; Daytona probe 8–33 sandbox-hours ≈ $4–66, quota-gated | Local $130–530; Daytona-scale 12.6k–52k sandbox-hours (≈ $6k–100k, weeks of quota) | 10–40 min local; hours on Daytona (quota ≤¼ RL org) | Local ~1–3 days; Daytona weeks under the quota cap | Flaky controls → wrong tier verdicts (retry policy bounds); under-exercising; quota exhaustion; infra errors need the existing retry classification |
| (d) Hybrid — static first, LLM residual, controls confirm | (a) over every task; (b) only where rules return "ambiguous"; route-changing confirmations ride the existing verification ladder | Rule receipts + ledger records for the residual + sampled verdicts | Union, bounded by the residual share; conservative by construction (only evidence-backed fields are written) | Static ≈ $0.02 + residual LLM ≈ $0.6–1.6 (10–30% of tasks) | **≈ $1–3k total, ~150–470k LLM tasks** | ~2 s + residual | **~1–2 days** | Union of the above, bounded by the residual threshold; ambiguous-set growth if rules are too narrow |

**Recommendation: (d).** Static-first because it is nearly free, fully evidenced, and its errors are safe in the conservative direction; the LLM pass only buys recall on the ambiguous residual; and control confirmation already exists in the ingest ladder, so a backfilled field is confirmed by the same fail-up mechanism without new cost. The scope addition's one-source pilot fits this: pick one Harbor-archive family, run (a), measure the ambiguous residual, then decide whether (b) is worth it at 1.58M scale.

## Workflow design: a requirement-backfill Atlas stage

**Placement.** A new `requirements` phase in `taskcompendium.pipeline.source_processing.run_source_pipeline`, between normalization and filtering: it runs as soon as Atlas has converted a source into TaskSpecs, and before verification so the control ladder routes on the backfilled fields. The curation driver passes the policy the way it passes review and controls settings (`SourcePipelineConfig`/`RecipeSettings` gains a `backfill` config: rule-set revision, LLM budget, residual threshold); the phase emits telemetry under `requirements/*` like the other phases. Nothing changes for sources whose specs already declare everything — the stage is idempotent and records "nothing to do".

**Inputs.** Normalized TaskSpec rows; the task's own bytes by role (`taskcompendium.runtime.resources.resource_inventory`, PR #11958 — scripts, `task.toml`, Dockerfiles); per-base image manifests (cached per pinned base, ~15 for the Harbor archives); optional GLM relay endpoint and budget for the residual; the backfill policy (rule-set revision, thresholds).

**Outputs.** TaskSpecs with evidence-backed fields. Each added field is written to the spec with its evidence: the field value plus a machine-readable evidence record (rule id and matched-file sha256 for the static pass; ledger record id and byte-verified quotes for the LLM pass) carried in the task's labels, so no TaskSpec schema change is needed and every downstream reader (route table, RL) sees declared fields exactly as today. Unresolved tasks keep "not stated" and therefore today's conservative route.

**Receipts.** A `requirements.json` manifest beside the filter and review manifests: per-source counts of field × rule × outcome (declared / unchanged / ambiguous / llm-proposed), LLM token and ledger summary, and the ambiguous-task set. The curation catalog gains matching backfill counts so Atlas shows per-source coverage next to admission counts. The pipeline identity hash includes the backfill policy revision, so a changed rule-set produces a new artifact identity through the existing `canonical_sha256` mechanism — re-ingesting under a new policy never silently overwrites an old one.

**Integration with tier routing.** Ingest already routes by the declared requirements with the conservative default (milestone 1) and fails up across the tier ladder with per-tier verdicts (milestone 2). Backfill only tightens declared fields, so a task's route changes only when its declared evidence says a cheaper tier suffices — and the sampled controls confirm it on the new route head through the same ladder, with no new machinery.

**Rollout.** Pilot on one Harbor-archive family (verifier scripts and Dockerfiles are in the payload): static pass, measure the residual, then price the LLM residual against the measured rate before committing to the full 1.56M.

## Taskforge tooling reused

**On main, reusable now:**
- `lib/taskforge/src/taskforge/spec/draft.py` — `requirements()` and `machine()`: the declaration vocabulary (semantics, capabilities, source, network `MachineSettings`) the backfill writes into.
- `lib/taskforge/src/taskforge/llm/` — `agent.py` (GLM-5.3 tool-calling agent loop), `glm_client.py` (retried chat client), `structured.py` (structured outputs), `recording.py` (`CallLedger`, the per-call evidence ledger), `client.py` (the `ModelClient` protocol).
- `lib/taskforge/src/taskforge/stage20_triage/checks.py` — the deterministic-check pattern (PASS/FAIL/SKIP with recorded false-positive/negative expectations) to copy for the static rules' receipts.
- `experiments/post_training/glm.py` — `GLM_MODEL` and the relay resolution the LLM residual rides on.
- `experiments/post_training/task_curation/environment_fidelity.py` — `lower_environment`/`PINNED_BASES`, already lowering Harbor Dockerfiles onto the ~15 pinned bases; the static pass reads its output rather than re-parsing images.

**From the author's unmerged work:**
- **PR #11958** (open, head `53861bd70e`, `mark/taskcompendium-resource-inventory`): `resource_inventory(task)` and `resource_signature` in `taskcompendium.runtime.resources` — every file a task carries by role with mode, sha256 and size. This is the static pass's primary input and should merge first.
- **Branch `mark/taskforge-stage50-validate`** (tip `eaaf49aa2e`, stacking `mark/taskforge-stage30-author` → `mark/taskforge-stage40-build-program` → stage50): `stage50_validate/control_drafts.py` (`write_controls` — LLM-drafted golden/negative controls validated against the grader's rejection ceiling, persisted to `controls.json`, replayable via `controls.replay`), `stage50_validate/trials.py` and `round.py` (trial execution and verdicts), `classify.py`/`outcome.py` (verdict classification), `evidence.py` (evidence records), and `lowering.py`. These are the confirm-by-controls machinery for the LLM residual and the pilot; `stage30_author`'s authoring loop (`loader.py`, `program.py`) is the prompt/agent pattern if the residual pass wants the full agent rather than one structured call.
- **PR #11947** (`mark/taskforge-s5-iris-timeout`, Iris sandbox survives a command timeout): orthogonal sandbox robustness; not needed for backfill since Iris is end-of-life as a tier. Worth landing on its own merits.
- **PR #11949** (decision-model grader kind): not on the backfill path — forge-main excludes the decision-model split, and the grader kind changes grading, not requirement declaration.
- The remaining ~65 `mark/taskforge-*` / `mark/forge-*` branches are the staged Forge lane pipeline (s0–s6, wp0–wp6, applets, canaries); nothing else on them is on the backfill critical path.

The sanctioned profile for in-pod sandbox graders is `container_profile_privileged` (`CONTAINER_PROFILE_PRIVILEGED` in the curation driver) — the same profile main's curation campaigns run their sandbox graders under. With that profile the local tier is expected to serve.

comments.author: penfever
comments.body:
🤖 Local tier on Iris pods: container-profile findings + fail-fast error (scope: comment thread + coordinator direction, 2026-11-22)

**Where the local tier runs, and which profile decides it.** Atlas ingest and RL both build their Shellbox factories *in-process* — the curation driver inside its worker pods, and RL's rollout workers inside the RL main job's Ray workers (`marinskyrl.task_machine_factories` runs in `skyrl_train`'s rollout workers; there is no separate task-machine pod). So the local tier's bwrap availability is decided by the **job's own container profile**:

- Atlas ingest: the driver submits workers with `--container-profile` defaulting to `CONTAINER_PROFILE_PRIVILEGED` (`task_curation/driver.py:94`, help text at `:449`), matching `task-curation.md`'s "in-pod sandbox graders" requirement. Ingest controls therefore can sandbox — the backfill lane's `SandboxUnavailable` verdicts came from jobs submitted with the **default** profile.
- RL rollout pods: the RL main's container profile is whatever `IrisSkyRLExecution.container_profile` sets (`lib/marin/src/marin/rl/skyrl.py:470`); it **defaults to `None` → Iris' `CONTAINER_PROFILE_UNSPECIFIED`** (`vendor/skyrl/cloud/iris/iris_backend.py:303`), and the rollout workers inherit the main job's pods. Launches that need in-pod sandbox graders must set `job_pb2.CONTAINER_PROFILE_PRIVILEGED` (`docs/references/rl-launching.md:212-216`, which also notes Iris requires admin authorization for the elevated profile). Production evidence: the quick-loop launch sets it (`experiments/post_training/inventory/train_quick_loop.py:213`). So **the local tier works in RL rollout pods only when the launch sets `CONTAINER_PROFILE_PRIVILEGED`**; a default-profile launch cannot run bwrap, and with the gVisor/Iris tier retired there is no fallback image tier except Daytona.
- Iris profile machinery for reference: `CONTAINER_PROFILE_PRIVILEGED` → `privileged=true` on the Docker/K8s runners (`lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/runtime/docker.py:285`); `CONTAINER_PROFILE_SANDBOX` is the gVisor path (`k8s/tasks.py:1253`).

**Fail-fast at construction.** The local factory already probes once at construction (`LocalMachineFactory.__init__` → `_working_bwrap`, which builds a real sandbox per candidate) — nothing about the tier ladder changed that. What was missing was the remedy in the error: `SandboxUnavailable` now also says, verbatim, *"On Iris, run the job with the CONTAINER_PROFILE_PRIVILEGED container profile, which grants these capabilities (submitting it needs admin authorization)."* The error surfaces at launch — `LocalGraderMachines`/`CampaignMachines` construct their factories when the driver builds machines, and RL's `task_machine_factories` constructs `LocalMachineFactory` when the rollout worker starts — so a mis-profiled pod dies with the typed error instead of failing per task. Behavior test added (`test_sandbox_unavailable_error_names_the_required_container_profile`). Commit `2a8fea17c1` on PR #11988.

**Not changed:** cluster configs, launch documents, or the router's tier order (per direction). If a future launch wants the local tier without PRIVILEGED, the fix is the launch profile, not the tier table.

spillover_issues.author: penfever
spillover_issues.body:
## TL;DR

A ~12-hour PRODUCTION-priority sprint (opened 2026-11-21 ~23:00 EST per the user request) to (1) maximize Snowball decode throughput at the 65,536-token request window and (2) size the Snowball RL job as small as possible while keeping training saturated (rollout wait near zero, no time-per-update regression vs the current baseline). Deliverable: a right-sized Snowball RL layout (GPU counts, engine config, all gates) with its measured time per update vs the current allocation and the GPU-hours cost per update. This issue is maintained by the secretary agent from the worker's REPORT.md/STATUS.md; every measured arm is recorded as it lands with reproduction details.

## Description

Context: Snowball RL runs on the Exp4/Exp5 long-loop pools (H100 on cw-rno2a; Snowball also ran on cw-us-east-08a GB200 for the Nov 20 acceptance, job `.305`, 40 GB200). The playbook and lessons come from the Mochi sprint (#11954, closed) and its concurrency-gate table (#11957).

Two phases:
- **Phase 1 — decode throughput at 65k context**: pure serving-benchmark arms with the exact Snowball RL rollout engine config, measured with native vLLM counters (aggregate and per-GPU generated tok/s, per-request tok/s, running/waiting per engine, KV use, prefix-hit rate, preemptions, TTFT) on a long-prompt 65,536-token workload with group-shared prompts as in RL.
- **Phase 2 — right-size the RL job**: shrink rollout GPUs and trainer GPUs step by step on real rollouts with the current Snowball curriculum (Exp4/Exp5 pools); report time per update, rollout wait, engine occupancy, and the per-step split (rollout wait / optimizer / checkpoint / eval). Saturated = trainer rollout wait per step near zero and time per update not regressing vs baseline.

Fixed infrastructure/rules for all arms: PRODUCTION priority; GPU budget ≤ ~2 racks / 128 GPUs in flight without coordinator approval; do not disturb Exp5 SFT (256 H100 on cw-rno2a); one knob per arm, config over code; each arm cancelled with `iris-cancel-own` once measured (25-min windows); Harbor ≤ 512 (Daytona RL org shared, one job ~1/4–1/3 of its 6,000 vCPU); long jobs' IDs go to the coordinator watchdog, no polling loops.

### Reproduction

- Repo: `marin-community/marin`, worktree `/Users/benfeuer/Documents/marin-worktrees/snowball-resize` (branch `benfeuer/snowball-resize` from the long-loop tip); all code/config lands ONLY via `loop-push` onto `benfeuer/long-loop-prototype` — no bespoke launchers.

## Conclusion

- Selected approach and evidence: **RIGHT-SIZED SNOWBALL RL LAYOUT (measured): 64 GB200 — trainer 8×4 nodes (Megatron PP2/CP4/EP4 all_gather, `dp_reshardable` checkpoints) + 4 rollout engines × DP8/EP8 at HBM 0.90, seqs 128, batched 8192; 16 rollout workers; all demand gates open (in-flight 1024, Harbor 384, verifier 384, tasks 2048, executor 384); staleness 2; curriculum-derived quotas 22/42; cadence-3; 30-min trajectory budgets — ~0.96 GPU-hour per update at batch 64.** Evidence chain: phase-1 decode sweeps (HBM 0.75→0.90 = 5.11× to 1,618.9 tok/s/GPU at the 65k window; seqs 64→128 = +16.5% to 1,886.4; KV must hold the shared-prompt working set); the phase-2 ladder on real rollouts (4 workers + closed gates 1,695.4 s at 90.2% wait → gates open 687.1 s → 16 workers **195.0 s/update at 13.4% wait**, 710.7 gen tok/s/GPU step-average, mismatch healthy 0.0060–0.0062) → **3 engines REGRESSED** (513.1 s at 72.8% wait — 24 rollout GPUs starve the trainer) → **trainer-shrink does not fit** (16 trainer ranks need ~269 GB/rank steady vs 192 GB GB200 HBM). 🤖
# Research

This is a production measurement campaign, not a discrete code defect. The issue currently records baseline collection in progress and no measured Snowball arms. The Mochi sprint found that staleness lookahead and Harbor slots could bind after engine tuning, so pure-serving throughput alone cannot select the RL layout ([#11954](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11954), [#11957](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11957)). No open PR claims #11969; [#11120](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11120) already owns the long-loop runner.

**Relevant code**
- [`throughput.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/2ca1e82187c630d0bfb305898f8baa9fa5b58977/experiments/post_training/long_loop/throughput.py#L103-L175): pinned serving sweep and receipts.
- [`round_runner.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/2ca1e82187c630d0bfb305898f8baa9fa5b58977/experiments/post_training/long_loop/round_runner.py#L700-L825): source-pinned round validation and launch.
- [`exp4.yaml`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/2ca1e82187c630d0bfb305898f8baa9fa5b58977/experiments/post_training/long_loop/rounds/exp4.yaml): current Exp4 round recipe.

# Plan

1. Record the active Snowball baseline from the worker's pinned source, resolved round, job ID, trainer and rollout GPU counts, engine TP/DP/EP, memory fraction, sequence and batch limits, and every effective concurrency gate. Measure completed update times, rollout wait, optimizer, checkpoint, and eval time on the current Exp4/Exp5 curriculum; publish the receipt before comparing arms.
2. Run 65,536-token serving arms with group-shared prompts and the baseline engine config through `throughput.py`. Change one of memory fraction, `max_num_seqs`, expert parallelism, or batched tokens per arm; keep 25-minute counter windows and report generated tokens/s per GPU, request rate, running/waiting, KV use, prefix hit, preemptions, and TTFT. Mark incomplete or error-heavy windows inconclusive; check any TP or quantization candidate against BF16 logprobs before using its rate.
3. Carry the best valid serving candidate into real rollouts, then reduce rollout GPUs and trainer GPUs one step at a time while holding curriculum, staleness, route quotas, and checkpoint/eval cadence fixed. Compare complete optimizer updates against the baseline; report rollout wait and the per-step time split, plus GPU-hours/update = total allocated GPUs × seconds/update ÷ 3600.
4. Select the smallest layout whose rollout wait remains near zero and whose update time does not regress within the observed variation. Publish the chosen GPU counts, full engine and gate configuration, source commit, launch commands, Iris IDs, Finelog windows, receipts, baseline comparison, and cost on this issue and the linked logbook. Keep the 128-GPU in-flight cap, Harbor ≤512, Exp5 SFT isolation, and own-job cancellation rules from the issue.

spillover_issues.author: penfever
spillover_issues.body:
RL launch reports only the first missing required environment variable, so users must repeat submission to find the full set.

Reproduce:
1. Construct an RL graph with one execution that requires `DAYTONA_TARGET` and another that requires `DAYTONA_EVAL_API_KEY`.
2. Remove both names from the submitting environment.
3. Invoke the graph entry point with `--run`.

The coordinator request indexes the environment one name at a time and raises `KeyError` for only the first missing name. This path exists on main in `lib/marin/src/marin/rl/cli.py`.

Expected: before submission or secret resolution, report all missing required names across the graph in one error. Do not include values. Forward all required values when they are present.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖

## Research

`_coordinator_request()` reads each execution's required name with `env_vars[name]`; the first absent name raises `KeyError` before the remaining executions are checked. The launch path calls it before opening the Iris client.

Relevant code: [`rl/cli.py#L140-L151`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/rl/cli.py#L140-L151) — environment selection; [`rl/cli.py#L191-L202`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/rl/cli.py#L191-L202) — submission order.

## Proposed Fix

Collect required names across the graph, report all absent names in one `click.UsageError` before selecting values, and keep forwarding the required values when present. Extend the launch test to cover two missing names and confirm that no request is submitted.

spillover_issues.author: penfever
spillover_issues.body:
A SkyRL evaluation on `cw-us-east-02a` selected Ethernet/RoCE HCAs and failed its launch-time collective gate on all 16 hosts.

Reproduce:
1. Submit a 16-node, 8-H100-per-node SkyRL generation job to `cw-us-east-02a` without an explicit `NCCL_IB_HCA` in the child request.
2. Run the standard all-GPU interconnect gate with the task runtime.
3. Inspect the per-task port inventories and retained rank errors.

The 16 inventories expose active `ibp0`–`ibp7` InfiniBand ports and `mlx5_0`–`mlx5_8` Ethernet ports. NCCL 2.32.6 selected both. Local GPU 4 on every host (global ranks 4, 12, …, 124) reported `IBV_WC_RETRY_EXC_ERR(12)` on Ethernet HCAs, with vendor error 129; one also reported `IBV_WC_WR_FLUSH_ERR(5)`. All 128 workers subsequently aborted and all 16 durable gate reports failed. This pattern does not isolate one defective host.

Expected: the child request selects the InfiniBand rails before both the gate and serving start. Keep explicit runtime settings authoritative and keep the gate strict.

#11749 already sets `NCCL_IB_HCA=ibp` in the canonical cluster configuration, but that selection was absent from this task's effective NCCL device selection. The SkyRL launcher currently supplies only an rno2a bootstrap default, so this job depended on deployment-time environment delivery. The proposed fix sends the existing `ibp` choice explicitly in east02a child requests. A child-request regression fails on the original source and passes with the fix; live qualification remains pending.

Related: #11618 and #11749.

SkyRL copies recipe `extra_env` into the child request’s `runtime.task_env`; an east02a request with no explicit HCA therefore omits `NCCL_IB_HCA`. The cluster config sets `NCCL_IB_HCA=ibp`, but the failed gate shows that setting was absent from this task’s effective device selection.

Relevant code: [child request construction](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/rl/skyrl.py#L1061-L1081), [east02a HCA config](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/config/cw-us-east-02a.yaml#L176-L181), [launcher task environment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/vendor/skyrl/cloud/iris/iris_backend.py#L882-L886).

## Proposed Fix

Set `NCCL_IB_HCA=ibp` in east02a child requests when `extra_env` does not specify it. Keep explicit recipe values authoritative and add a child-request regression covering the default and override.

spillover_issues.author: Helw150
spillover_issues.body:
🤖 The general form of the harness-robustness dream eval: run any lm-eval-harness benchmark inside real agent harnesses and measure how much accuracy each model conserves in-harness ("can model X solve simple benchmark Y in harness Z?"). #7169 is the static, hand-built first step (MMLU/GSM8K/HumanEval in one minimal contract); this issue is the machinery that makes it automatic. Related to the evals wish-list in #7090.

## Motivation

Benchmark accuracy measured by raw completion or chat Q&A does not predict accuracy through an agentic harness — models differ sharply in how much they conserve (Qwen 3 conserves most of its accuracy in-harness; Qwen 2.5 / Llama 3 do not). Making every existing lm-eval-harness benchmark runnable in-harness turns the whole benchmark corpus into a harness-robustness probe for free.

## Approach: a generic Harbor adapter

Harbor already has the right extension point: the [`adapters/`](https://github.com/laude-institute/harbor/tree/main/adapters) directory contains ~85 per-benchmark adapters (aime, mmmlu, humanevalfix, bfcl, arc_agi_2, …), each a package that downloads a source benchmark and generates Harbor tasks following shared conventions — dockerized per-task environments, oracle solutions, agents writing their answer to `/app/answer.txt`, and tests verifying the answer.

Rather than hand-writing one adapter per benchmark, this issue proposes **one generic `lm_eval` adapter, parameterized by lm-eval-harness task name**:

- **Input**: an lm-eval task identifier (e.g. `gsm8k`, `mmlu_abstract_algebra`, `humaneval`). The adapter resolves the task's dataset, prompt rendering (`doc_to_text`), gold target (`doc_to_target`), and metric config from lm-eval's own task registry.
- **Task generation**: each doc becomes a Harbor task — instruction = rendered prompt + the standard answer-channel sentence; environment = minimal Ubuntu/Python container (sandboxed test runner for code tasks); oracle = writes the gold answer.
- **Verifier**: the lm-eval metric applied to `/app/answer.txt` contents (exact match / regex extraction / unit-test execution), reusing lm-eval's metric code where possible so scoring stays parity-comparable with native runs.
- **Conventions**: follow the existing adapter template (README with provenance/scope/modifications, auto data download, per-task isolation) so it can be upstreamed to harbor.

Existing per-benchmark adapters (aime, mmmlu, humanevalfix) validate the pattern; the generic adapter subsumes future hand-porting for anything already in lm-eval's registry.

## Metric

Per (model, benchmark, harness): in-harness accuracy vs. native lm-eval accuracy → a **harness conservation ratio**. Sweep harnesses (Terminus-2-style bare JSON+bash, a Claude-Code-like stack, others Harbor supports) to get a robustness profile rather than a single number.

## Scoping / phasing

1. **Phase 1 — `generate_until` tasks with mechanical metrics** (GSM8K, triviaqa-style exact match): cleanest translation.
2. **Phase 2 — multiple-choice tasks** (MMLU, ARC): native lm-eval scores these by loglikelihood over options, which has no in-harness equivalent — the converted task submits a choice letter instead. The conversion changes what's measured (generative vs. discriminative), so report as a separate track, not a like-for-like delta.
3. **Phase 3 — execution-verified tasks** (HumanEval, MBPP): unit tests run in the container; optionally allow k repair turns as a difficulty ladder.

## Open questions

- Few-shot handling: keep lm-eval's few-shot examples in the instruction (simpler, keeps parity) vs. re-rendering as episodes.
- Answer-extraction parity: lm-eval extraction regexes are tuned for completion output; the answer channel makes extraction trivial — decide whether native baselines should be recomputed under a strict answer-channel protocol for fairness.
- Cost: full MMLU in-harness is expensive; support seeded subsampling (tinyBenchmarks-style) for the sweep matrix.
- ~~Upstreaming: target `harbor/adapters/lm_eval` upstream vs. incubating in marin first.~~ Resolved: develop in the existing fork at [marin-community/harbor](https://github.com/marin-community/harbor) (`adapters/lm_eval/`), then PR upstream to harbor-framework/harbor once the phase-1 tasks validate. evalchemy tasks (a superset wrapping lm-eval) could be a follow-up source format.

## Deliverables

1. The generic `lm_eval` Harbor adapter (task name in → Harbor task dir out), following upstream adapter conventions.
2. Generated task sets for a starter suite (GSM8K, MMLU, HumanEval — superseding the hand-built #7169 once parity is shown).
3. A harness-conservation report across the model suite and ≥2 harnesses.

comments.author: claude[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 **Analysis — not opening a PR.** This is a new multi-module feature (converter + task sets + report, 3 phases). Posting root-cause/design for human sign-off before implementation, per the fix-issue scope rule.

# Research

The Harbor *runner* side already exists and is generic; what's missing is the *authoring* side — a tool that emits Harbor task directories from lm-eval task definitions. `HarborEvaluator` already loads a local directory of Harbor tasks (`LocalDatasetConfig(path=...)`) or an HF snapshot (`hf://…`), runs them in Docker/Daytona, and aggregates per-task reward→accuracy. So a converter that writes a task dir per doc plugs straight into the existing evaluator with zero runner changes. The native baseline path (`simple_evaluate`) is also already wired, giving the "raw" side of the harness delta for free.

**Relevant code**
- [`harbor_evaluator.py#L384-L430`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/evaluators/harbor_evaluator.py#L384-L430) — local-dir / `hf://` / registry dataset selection (converter output target)
- [`harbor_evaluator.py#L481-L521`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/evaluators/harbor_evaluator.py#L481-L521) — reads each task's `verifier_result.rewards.reward`; the converted task's verifier just needs to emit this
- [`evals.py#L391`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/evals/evals.py#L391) — `evaluate_harbor(...)`; `dataset=` already accepts a local path
- [`lm_evaluation_harness_evaluator.py#L110-L121`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/evaluators/lm_evaluation_harness_evaluator.py#L110-L121) — `simple_evaluate` native baseline (the "raw" score for the delta)
- #7169 — static, hand-built MMLU/GSM8K/HumanEval defining the answer-channel contract this converter should reproduce mechanically

# Proposed approach

**Converter = read lm-eval task → write a Harbor task dir per doc.** Live marin-side under `lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/` (a `harbor_convert/` module); consider upstreaming to Harbor only after the contract stabilizes.

Read task defs through lm-eval's own registry (`lm_eval.tasks.get_task_dict(name)`), which exposes `doc_to_text`, `doc_to_target`, the dataset docs, and metric config — don't reparse YAML. Per doc emit:
- **instruction** ← rendered `doc_to_text` (+ few-shot context) + one standard sentence naming the answer channel.
- **environment** ← minimal image for text tasks; the existing sandboxed code runner for code tasks.
- **answer channel** ← single contract, write final answer to `/answer.txt` (mirror #7169's `submit_answer`/EOS discipline so the two can be reconciled).
- **verifier** ← the lm-eval metric applied to the submitted answer vs `doc_to_target` gold, emitting `reward` in the shape the evaluator already reads.

**Phasing** (matches the issue):
1. `generate_until` + mechanical metric (GSM8K, exact-match) — cleanest, no like-for-like caveat.
2. Multiple-choice (MMLU/ARC) — native scoring is loglikelihood-over-options with no in-harness analog; the converted task submits a choice letter. Report as a **separate track**, not a like-for-like delta.
3. Execution-verified (HumanEval/MBPP) — reuse the existing HumanEval sandbox runner as the verifier; optional k repair turns as a difficulty ladder.

**Open-question recommendations**
- *Few-shot*: keep lm-eval's examples inline in the instruction — simpler and preserves parity.
- *Extraction parity*: Phase 1 report native lm-eval as-is with an explicit caveat; recompute the native baseline under the strict answer-channel protocol only if the delta proves extraction-dominated (defer, don't build up front).
- *Cost*: deterministic per-task subsampling with a fixed seed at materialization time (tinyBenchmarks-style); lm-eval `limit` is sample-order, not stable across tasks, so subsample in the converter.
- *Location*: marin-side first (above); upstream later.

**Recommended first PR** (reviewable slice, not the whole thing): Phase 1 converter for a single `generate_until` task (GSM8K) → local Harbor task dir → run through `evaluate_harbor`, plus one behavior test asserting a known-correct answer scores reward 1.0 and a wrong one 0.0 through the emitted verifier. Everything else lands incrementally on that spine.

Flagging for a human to confirm module placement (marin-side vs. upstream Harbor) and the answer-channel contract before I start Phase 1.
