spillover_issues.author: flufcloud
spillover_issues.body:
Note: All text that follows was written by me with no AI-assistance :-)
# Overview

We would like to understand the influence of duplicated data on model performance and scaling laws. Prior work has identified that ‘duplicated data’ is hiding a lot of complexity: *how* the data is duplicated has a lot of impact on model scaling.

For instance, Hernandez et. al. find that the distribution of duplicated data influences how models scale. In particular, they find that for the same fraction of duplicated data,  repeating either a small sample of data many times or a big sample of data a few times has minimal effect on scaling, while a medium sample of data repeated a medium amount has stark negative effects. Kazdan et. al. find that semantic collisions are more harmful as the dataset and model size scale. They further note that in the training regime that contains many semantic collisions, scaling laws can break down unexpectedly (they provide an auxiliary term that mostly repairs them).

This motivates a rigorous study of how duplicated data influences model performance. We ask
* How does the mix of duplicated data affect how models scale?
* How does model scaling differ across different methods for deduplication, such as exact, fuzzy, and semantic?
* Are there cases in which duplicating quality data is better for training than other unique, but lower quality, data?
  * If so, how can we easily identify such data? For example, is the degree of duplication of some datapoint an indicator on how useful that datapoint is?

Studying these questions can motivate principled changes to Marin’s data standardization pipeline.

# Previous Experiments & Links

* [[Original Datakit Testbed Spec](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/c9dbd2709ad59fe2ee2f2833e5de19f474090802/docs/design/datakit_testbed.md)](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/c9dbd2709ad59fe2ee2f2833e5de19f474090802/docs/design/datakit_testbed.md)
* [[Initial Experiments](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/5200)](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/5200)
  * The experiments setup 3 model training runs
    * A baseline run, where data is sampled naturally with no deduplication applied
    * A fuzzy deduplication run, where data is sampled and then a dedupe pass is applied (this was slightly better than the baseline)
    * A run with 50% of the sampled data repeated (this was around the same performance as the baseline)

# Proposed Experiments

I have a few ideas

* Since the run with 50% duplicated data (equivalently, the run with 50% unique data) did not perform worse, we should push until we find how much unique data we need. We launch runs that use 25% unique data, 10% unique data, and 5% unique data and measure how performance is lost
  * Hypothesis: We’ll see a sort of power law where models get exponentially worse
  * We should properly regularize to make it fair, following from prior work by Kim et. al.
* Produce a scaling law curve for each of the 3 existing runs
  * Hypothesis: the curvature of the curves will be different, which might imply sensitivity to duplication
* There has been discussion on data that is superficially duplicate (e.g., templated data). What if the degree of duplication is a useful proxy for data quality? We can identify the top-N most duplicated data points in the testbed and remove them completely (not even leaving a unique version of it), ablating with the fuzzy dedup and baseline runs.
  * Hypothesis: highly repeated data (as calculated by the fuzzy dedup strategy) is actually not very useful

Other ideas include following up on the work on KRR and DSP predictions, investigating the robustness of simulated epoching scaling patterns when extrapolated to the full training run, or other connections to data mix.

# References

* Scale Dependent Data Duplication: Kazdan, J., Levi, N., Schaeffer, R., Chudnovsky, J., Puri, A., He, B., Donmez, M., Koyejo, S., & Donoho, D. (2026). Scale Dependent Data Duplication. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.06603
* Pre-training under infinite compute: Kim, K., Kotha, S., Liang, P., & Hashimoto, T. (2025). Pre-training under infinite compute. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.14786
* Scaling Data-Constrained Language Models: Muennighoff, N., Rush, A. M., Barak, B., Le Scao, T., Piktus, A., Tazi, N., Pyysalo, S., Wolf, T., & Raffel, C. (2023). Scaling Data-Constrained Language Models. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.16264
* Larger Datasets Can Be Repeated More: Yan, T., et al. (2025). Larger Datasets Can Be Repeated More: A Theoretical Analysis of Multi-Epoch Scaling in Linear Regression. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.13421
* Scaling Laws and Interpretability of Learning from Repeated Data: Hernandez, D., et al. (2022). Scaling Laws and Interpretability of Learning from Repeated Data. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.10487

spillover_issues.author: rjpower
spillover_issues.body:
The Marin codebase needs to maintain a high level of quality to preserve development velocity. As agents have increased the rate of code production, the burden of doing code reviews has increased as well. While we don't demand code review for every PR, we still rely on it for important new code additions and to ensure code fits our guidelines.

One area we're particularly concerned about is slop. Agents produce "slop" in a way and scope well beyond a normal human coder: documentation or comments written in a bizarre style, oddly baroque abstractions, or repetitive coding practices. As a reviewer, it's frustrating and tiring to have to comment on slop code.

We have an initial set of agentic linting rules tied into our commit process that were mostly created from scratch. This proposes a weekly process to automatically refine and improve these rules based on observed reviewer feedback: rules which have never triggered are removed, and new rules introduced to capture common patterns, measured automatically and rolled out against a benchmarking set to ensure we don't regress.

## Current status

Our review process tracks findings by rule and user. Currently 3,672 findings across 61 distinct rules; the top 12 rules account for ~62% of findings, with the remaining 49 rules accounting for 37.4% (1,373).

Top rules by finding count:

| Rule | Findings | Share |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| ml-tuple-return-shape | 285 | 7.8% |
| ml-duplicate-logic-block | 277 | 7.5% |
| ml-magic-constant | 245 | 6.7% |
| ml-overloaded-function | 245 | 6.7% |
| ml-impl-narration-docstring | 244 | 6.6% |
| ml-slop-test | 243 | 6.6% |
| ml-unused-param | 216 | 5.9% |
| ml-echo-across-files | 154 | 4.2% |
| ml-module-globals | 108 | 2.9% |
| ml-env-var-vs-param | 97 | 2.6% |
| ml-duplicate-constant | 93 | 2.5% |
| ml-misleading-name | 92 | 2.5% |
| Remaining 49 rules | 1,373 | 37.4% |

A spot review shows these reviews are almost always acted on by the development agent, implying even the ad-hoc reviews have saved thousands of user interactions. Despite this, we still regularly post PRs full of agentic slop, with plenty of room for improvement.

## Proposal

Two levers:

- **Better enforcement:** auto-reject PRs that don't have the `agentic-review` tag assigned to them. This should force agents that forgot the agentic review process to trigger review.
- **Better quality:** every human comment on a PR is something that *could* have been caught during agentic PR review. Analyze these weekly and identify the comment types that recur most frequently and are easiest to resolve.

## Approach

- Move statistics out of WandB and into Finelog via a bulk import & CLI adjustments
- Add a Grafana dashboard for monitoring & alerting rules as appropriate
- Set up a weekly GitHub action which:
  - **Fetch:** all PRs with comments in the last week
  - **Triage:** which comments are actionable for linting
  - **Review:** which rules haven't fired for > 1 month
  - **Adopt:** new rules which would have captured the failure patterns

## Success criteria

- A live dashboard on Grafana showing agentic code review feedback statistics, including triggers, feedback quality metrics, timing (too slow a feedback loop and users get impatient), and any issues we run into
- Weekly report sent to Slack with our PR statistics
- A codified, tentatively weekly, auto-improvement process for our agentic linting patterns

Long-term success metric: *does the number of PR comments that could have been caught by agentic linting go down over time?* This is not a hard metric — it will fluctuate as coding standards change and as agents get more powerful — but in general we want to see it go down.

## Rollout

Bulk upload of all agentic lint data into Finelog with the initial rollout, then set up GitHub actions for the maintenance loop.

## Expected timeframe

~1 day of work, which can be overlapped with other ongoing projects.

## Alternatives considered

**Do nothing.** Rejected: this is a low-effort way to reduce human reviewer load.

**Adopt some external service.** Rejected: lack of a self-reinforcement cycle, and an initial survey found no external service provided significantly higher value.

spillover_issues.author: jamt9000
spillover_issues.body:
As of #7820 the expert FF parameters are stored in a big `[n_layers, n_experts, d_in, d_out]` tensor, eg `[48, 384, 3072, 3072]`, with the specialised [`_newtonschulz_4d_distributed`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/5da0277745729230801f91e0181406f291099f9d/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/grugmuon_hero.py#L211) computing Newton Schulz on the last two dimensions.

However, in the optimizer, the axes used to compute the norm will end up as `(1,2,3)`, which includes the expert dimension.

https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/5da0277745729230801f91e0181406f291099f9d/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/optimizer.py#L76

This seems to be unintentional, since that optimizer code was originally to handle 3D `[n_experts, d_in, d_out]` shapes in #6153.

The implication is that an updated matrix parameter **M**<sub>t+1</sub> will **no longer be constrained to its original hypersphere** of norm ||**M**<sub>t</sub>||<sub>F</sub> as described in MuonH originally. Instead the combined cat([**M**<sub>t+1</sub><sup>expert1</sup>, **M**<sub>t+1</sub><sup>expert2</sup>, ...]) will be constrained to norm ||cat([**M**<sub>t</sub><sup>expert1</sup>, **M**<sub>t</sub><sup>expert2</sup>, ...])||<sub>F</sub> allowing individual matrices to grow or shrink within that constraint. Although not necessarily a terrible thing to do (experiments in https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/5253 tried both for AdamH).

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body: Great find. Yes, this is unintentional. Given that our prior tests across 4 scales showed negligible impact (actually slightly better) with norm computation over all experts at once, will leave in and let the run continue.

The first 4 layers see a spread. I think its conceptually reasonable to think of all routed experts as a single matrix that is sparsely activated for each token. Though NS is ran per expert, so this blurs the representation.

I was having similar thoughts, it's interesting how Muon basically treats any matrix-shaped thing as a matrix when some of that is down to data layout decisions on whether to pack multiple logical matrices into one. spillover_issues.author: marianna13
spillover_issues.body: # Hypothesis / goal H0: Short RL training (<200 steps) cannot teach a task-specific skill but only re-usable skills (e.g. using agentic harness). H1: RL does teach task-specific skills. # Method Definitions: - We call transferrable (or re-usable skills) a capabilities that can be applied to different tasks and do not depend on the specific task context. Examples: tool usage, efficient context usage etc. - On the other hand, the skills that are only useful for specific tasks we will call task-specific. They help with certain tasks/contexts but cannot be applied universally and therefore are not helpful in general. To determine whether RL only teaches transferrable skills we conduct following experiments: - Exp 1: RL on the non-agentic base. Non-agentic model is not familiar with the specific harness, so RL needs to teach this capability first. If RL is capable of pushing task-specific skill further we should see continuous improvement in pass@1 (reward). However, if RL only teaches how to use the harness we would expect rising reward in the beginning and then plateau (model effectively learned how to use the harness but it doesn't improve in actual task solution and RL exhausted what it can squeeze from the policy). Note: this does not mean that it's the case (it can be something else like exploration collapse) but it's one evidence that will count towards H0. Therefore, exp 1 on it's own is not enough to disprove H1. - Exp 2: RL on agentic base (already knows how to use the harness). Evidence for H1: reward should climb - RL can teach capability beyond harness usage. If reward is flat it's another evidence towards H0. - Exp 3: RL on agentic base with a different harness. If H0 holds, the behavior should be similar to Exp 1 - reward rises up in the beginning and thne plateaus. - Exp 4: RL that rewards transferrable skills beyond harness usage. Construct tasks that require some re-usable skill in order to solve and reward the model for efficient usage of that skill. Rising reward here would also support H0 (though is not a clear evidence against H1). All together Exp. 1-4 should provide enough evidence to prove or disprove H0. We don't test RL transfer (i.e. agent performance on OOD tasks) since we only care about training dynamics and the transfer is a separate question. # Status In the process of consolidating the empirical evidence. ## Exp 1 Qwen3-8B (no agentic) on [code-contests](https://huggingface.co/datasets/DCAgent/code-contests-noblock) dataset and terminus-2 harness. We see rapid increase in training reward in just 15 steps in the beginning and then a plateau. This behavior is consistent with "the non-agentic model first learned how to use the harness and how to behave in the agentic workflows". Then RL just stops being useful. For comparison, I also did the same setup but [g1](https://huggingface.co/DCAgent/g1_diverse_tezos_100k_8b) (agentic SFT on top of Qwen3-8B). We see that for SFT'ed model there's no improvement (even a small decrease) in reward where the base was improving. Importantly, g1 starts where base finishes (0.30 -> 0.50 by step 15). However, both improve their token efficiency (base -10% and g1 -15% in avg response length), this is supports H0 - a systematic behavioral skill that RL can teach a model. ## Exp 2 Ran [g1](https://huggingface.co/DCAgent/g1_diverse_tezos_100k_8b) (Qwen3-8B trained on teacher traces with terminus-2 harness) on R2E-Gym dataset with ctx len 81k (yarn factor=2). Harness: terminus-2 (t2) - native for g1. Longer context was used because for r2e tasks and terminus-2 more than half of rollouts are useless - they crash with CLE. Trained for 84 steps. Reward over 84 steps: 0.326->0.375, p@8: 0.516->0.609. The reward slope shrinks from +0.00086 to +0.00032/step as more steps are added (a plateau), not a slow climb that just needed room. pass@8 is visibly pinned at ~0.60 from step 10 onward. There's areal policy movement shown by KL climbing but almost no improvement in pass rate. ## Exp 3 Same configuration as Exp 2 but with terminus-structured harness and native 40k ctx len for Qwen (t-struct has better context management than t2 ). Trained for 140 steps. Reward over 140 steps: 0.24 -> 0.35 (almost the same p@1 as g1 on t2 starts from i.e. no real capability gain). p@: 0.47->0.58 (again g1 t2 starts at 0.58). ## Exp 4 [g1](https://huggingface.co/DCAgent/g1_diverse_tezos_100k_8b) on [SWE-smith-py-code-search](https://huggingface.co/datasets/OpenHands/SWE-smith-py-code-search). The task is code localization and not bug fixes. The reward function is $R=R^{F1-file}+R^{F1-module}+R^{F1-entity}$ sum of F1 scores for each granularity (file-, module-, entity-based localization). We see that for g1 the reward monotonically grows - the model learns to efferently search and at the same time becomes more efficient (avg response length drops). For each granularity level, we see that entity-level is the hardest and the steepest while file-level is almost saturated. Interestingly entity-level continues # Links - consolidated logs (Claude-generated): [link](https://huggingface.co/datasets/laion/rl-analysis-issue-8481) # Conclusion In all RL runs where reward is growing we see similar behavior - first it goes up and then plateaus. All exp.1-4 provide support for H0 and there's no counterexample. So we don't have enough evidence to reject H0 so

spillover_issues.title: [experiment, agentic RL] investigate what short-horizon agentic RL on small models can teach

spillover_issues.author: muchanem
spillover_issues.body:
Relevant work: #6521, [MATES](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.06046), [Group-MATES](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.14709), [RegMix](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.01492v2), [RegMix-D](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18663), [Meta-rater](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.14194), [DataMan](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.19363), [Scalable Influence and Fact Tracing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.17413), [DoGE](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.15393v2)

tl;dr: We should label our data on a bunch of axes (downstream performance, LLM oracle, gradient alignment, etc) and cluster over those axes (and domain) to create buckets for the data mixing swarms

The literature on pre-training data selection has moved fairly significantly beyond FineWeb-Edu style pipelines where you use an LLM-as-judge to rate a sample set of your pretraining data and then train a small model to predict those scalar labels across your pretraining data. 

The first and most important change is treating quality as a multi-dimensional label. In DataMan 14 quality criteria and 15 domains labels are used; in Meta-rater data is labeled on professionalism, readability, reasoning, and cleanliness and proxy models are trained to learn the most useful combination of the signals for validation loss. A scale-up of this approach looks like [propella-1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.12414v1)--Qwen3 models which produce structured JSON over 18 properties in six categories. 

The second change is moving to approaches that don't rely on an LLM oracle like downstream performance or gradient alignment. This changes include the further insight that these labels are dynamic (treating each label as conditional on training state/progress). For instance, MATES calculates loss of a model at step t after training on candidate points. DoGE calculates a gradient alignment for full domain buckets.

New work on pretraining data selection has also emphasized the importance of diversity and group-level view of utility. Group-MATES shows that the influence scores of documents cannot be considered independently, and groups documents using their individual influence scores. [Spokes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.15216) emphasizes the importance of diversity as a set-level attribute, meaning that buckets themselves should likely get labels as well.

The goal then is a vector of labels per training document, which then get clustered into groups, which can be selected over by our swarms.

Our particular setting and fusing the prior work into one pipeline introduces a few questions but also resolves a few difficulties:
* We are only trying to produce buckets: Meta-rater and Group-MATES think about both the labels and how to select over the labels, we only need to produce the most informative labels possible
* We will/do have training trajectories from model trained over substantially similar data to (presumably) what we will train on in the future. This potentially gives us more signal for model-based labels. However, naively using our checkpoints introduces the danger of only incorporating a memorization/exposure signal rather than a data property itself
* Should our clusters be independent of domain or include domain as another label? (my prior is domain should be included to create clusters)
* The cost and "unity" of the labeler:
   * We could do something like propella-1 where we have a fairly large model predict our entire vector at once. However, this means we introduce a large global barrier into quality labeling work: we can get labels once all have been finalized and the labeler is trained<sup>*</sup>. Additionally, we introduce ~5,000 B200-GPU hours of cost (1B labeler, FP4) to label our training set
   * Alternatively, we train models for each axis we care about at ~the size of our current quality labeler (40M). This allows work on axes to not block each other, but at 20 axes (pessimistically 12 due to small model MFUs) we end up using the same number of GPU hours, for a presumably worse result than predicting all axes at once with a larger model


\* Something like training LoRAs per axis and folding them into the model as we add new axes could work as we expand our set of labels, but also means introducing additional risk as we are stacking multiple bets at once when moving to this approach

comments.author: Helw150
comments.body: As a straw man, what info would you think this would capture that we can't capture from an affine projection from the embeddings we have from Harrier?

comments.author: muchanem
comments.body: A lot of the information is probably directly linearly decodable from the embeddings and doesn't require training a separate model (e.g. for the quality labels, like 90% of the performance of our current model can be captured by a linear probe on the document embedding). But, it's important that the projection be learned--the dominant variance in the embeddings is topic/genre, and so clustering on the embeddings directly (or after a random projection) wouldn't recover things like the MATES downstream performance metric or gradient alignment. So the labels can be understood as making the axes we care about dominant under the clustering metric rather than averaged out. I do also suspect some axes may also turn out to have no signal above label noise in Harrier at all, so we would need to train a separate model.

comments.author: Helw150
comments.body:
Sounds good! Yeah, I think the baseline would be to try your workflow for quality on other axes we care about and only expand to a custom model for axes we have high confidence & evidence will lead to improvements.

The fact that the expensive compute isn't re-usable is what I don't like about the Propella approach. If every time you want to add a new axis you need to re-run a full Qwen model pass over all your data, you'll quickly find yourself avoiding adding new axes because it's expensive and we're unlikely to get the axes right from the get go!

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
I am not well-read in datamixing literature and what actually works- but just a general thought on optimization.

In any open-ended optimization problem, a big decision is how to coalesce the search space into a tractable number of degrees of freedom (EG should we have a learning rate per parameter, or one global LR, or a learning rate per parameter per step). 

To me, every degree of freedom is inherently a bad thing. It exponentially grows the search space, increases risk of overfitting, and makes it harder to interpret results. And it is only worth including a degree of freedom when it empirically proves its worth. I also find it easy to underestimate the future inertia that degrees of freedom introduce. (EG if we fit a unique LR to MLP up projection, suddenly moving to Latent MoE means there is a lot more work to do to retune).

On DataMan 14 quality criteria, my first thought would be "how many of these can we remove without significantly hurting performance". I think its great to test a very large number of hypothesis during exploration phase, but afterwards, every degree of freedom of the system should be sensitive to the objective function- otherwise it should be pruned. I think its easy to get into the reverse mindset, where degrees of freedom are viewed as implying sophistication of the system (but I think this is backwards).

comments.author: muchanem
comments.body: I largely agree--I think the final design will include a step of clustering over all (or all but domain) of the axes, so our search space should stay small and ideally reducing risk of overfitting. spillover_issues.author: ravwojdyla-agent
spillover_issues.body:
## Description

Build **smallquery**: self-serve, BigQuery-like SQL analytics over our Parquet datasets on object storage (regional GCS and CoreWeave), running on Iris and using spare capacity on preemptible VMs. A user submits a SQL query through an API or dashboard and gets the result back in object storage to stream or download.

Design and implementation notes (the *how*) live in `.agents/projects/smallquery/` and `lib/smallquery/`. This issue tracks the **system requirements**, not the design.

## System requirements

- **Distributed execution with shuffle** — must run joins and high-cardinality `GROUP BY` across many workers, not single-node only. (Hard requirement.)
- **Preemption-tolerant** — workers run on preemptible VMs that can vanish at any moment; a query must still complete with correct results, without restarting from scratch.
- **Scales beyond one node** — handles queries whose working set exceeds a single VM's memory.
- **Opportunistic / good neighbour** — uses spare CPU/RAM and yields to higher-priority work; never starves co-located jobs.
- **Data-local, egress-aware** — computes in the same region/cloud as the data; rejects (or explicitly gates) queries that would cause cross-region egress.
- **Durable results** — materializes the full result to object storage (stream/download) plus a quick, size-capped inline preview.
- **Self-serve access** — a query API and a dashboard reachable on the Iris cluster.
- **Governed access** — datasets referenced by name through a catalog with per-dataset authorization; no raw object-store paths in user SQL (potentially integrated with the artifact registry).
- **Correct** — results match a single-node reference engine over the same data.

## Dependencies

- A per-node worker-fleet capability on Iris (#6763).

## Definition of Done (capabilities)

- [ ] A join and a high-cardinality `GROUP BY` run **distributed** and return correct results.
- [ ] Killing workers mid-query does not fail or corrupt the query — it still returns the correct result.
- [ ] Runs on spare/preemptible capacity and yields to higher-priority jobs.
- [ ] Results land in object storage and are reachable via the API + dashboard on both GCS and CoreWeave.
- [ ] Cross-region queries are rejected or explicitly gated per the egress policy.
- [ ] Results validated equal to a single-node reference.
- [ ] Design doc reviewed/merged.

comments.author: ravwojdyla-agent
comments.body:
The option in one picture: a persistent non-preemptible coordinator (API + dashboard) + a fleet of warm preemptible workers; queries become a DAG of shards that exchange chunks through object storage (never local disk); results to a TTL'd location + capped preview.

Key choices — each had a real alternative:
- Distributed + object-store shuffle ↔ single-node big-RAM (evaluated, rejected — distributed was a hard requirement; cf. https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/6760)
- Object-store shuffle ↔ local-disk shuffle on an SSD scratch group (would unlock off-the-shelf Spark/Trino).
- New IrisDaemon per-node primitive ↔ standing pool / per-query jobs.
- Per-attempt _SUCCESS manifest committer ↔ atomic-rename / conditional-create.
- Thin coordinator + embedded SQLite snapshotted to GCS ↔ reconcile-by-listing / Postgres.
- Kernel: DataFusion vs DuckDB left as a measured bake-off.
- Python coordinator (logical-plan cutting) + Rust workers ↔ Rust coordinator shipping physical plans.
- Skew: fail cheaply ↔ salting/spill.

Prior art: borrowed finelog (deployment/dashboard/SQLite-checkpoint) and zephyr (object-store scatter, retry tiers); the Spice AI Ballista fork is the only OSS object-store shuffle but recomputes durable data on writer loss (our committer avoids that); ClickHouse/smallpond/Polars rejected for our constraints.

One practically and lazy option would be to borrow useful parts/components of DataFusion/Ballista and sprinkle it with parts that require custom handling.

Worth noting the [limitations of distributed-datafusion](https://datafusion-contrib.github.io/datafusion-distributed/index.html#when-not-to-use-this-library), specifically:
> * If any node fails mid-query, the whole query fails; there are no retries.
> * There’s no persistence of intermediate results, so queries can’t checkpoint or resume from where they stopped.

This is probably fine for the interactive workload, but this is the trap that our preemptable infra sets and it would be worth analyzing query runtime vs. node preemption to see what percentage of queries would fail and at what scale it becomes unusable.

comments.author: alxmrs
comments.body:
Here are my thoughts and impressions about which technology choices to make for the smallquery project: 

## DuckDB vs Polars vs DataFusion

These are all very similar but I think there are some important  differences that will lead us to decide that DataFusion is the right RDBMS engine to build atop of. 

Here is DataFusion's explanation of the differences between each project: https://datafusion.apache.org/user-guide/faq.html#how-does-datafusion-compare-with-xyz

- DuckDB vs DataFusion: Both are very similar in goal (in process/embeddable OLAP query engine). DuckDB is built around its own internal format whereas DataFusion is designed to be agnostic of the core DB format. 
- DuckDB vs DataFusion: Both are modular and extensible, but DataFusion is the natural ancestor to Apache Arrow; see this post on [Composable Data Systems](https://wesmckinney.com/blog/looking-back-15-years/)
- DuckDB vs (DataFusion & Polars): C++ (sometimes, with Rust Extensions) vs a pure-rust ecosystem -- my preference is to go with Rust.
- Polars vs the rest: Polars is built on arrow, but is not designed as a "deconstructed database" like DuckDB and DataFusion, so it will be harder to integrate with. 

## Distribution 

Assuming DataFusion is the bet we go with, the next open question is Comet vs Ballista vs DataFusion Distributed: 

- Comet is DataFusion/Arrow within Spark, so I see this as really saying we should go with (better) Spark. While this is faster than Spark, it is still the slowest option in the distributed DataFusion ecosystem. This is lowest on my list, primarily because it adds a lot of system complexity (I count ~4-5 layers of abstraction between Zephyr, Spark, Comet, DataFusion, and Iris). The benefit, however, is that Comet happened to be a more popular choice than Ballista, even though I think Ballista is a better system. I think this might have to do with the amount of buy-in/popularity of Apache Spark.
- Ballista is the most mature way of distributing DataFusion. However, the DataFusion-Python to Ballista Python integration is somewhat far behind the primary version of DataFusion, making it suspect for us to want to depend on. (Warning: I could be wrong about this impression -- this is from recently trying to build on top of Ballista with Python a few months ago).
- DataFusion-Distributed is the new distributed system for DataFusion, and its core promise is to be a natural extension of the DataFusion data model (logical and physical plans). https://datafusion-contrib.github.io/datafusion-distributed/. I like this choice for Iris because it delegates full control over how plans are distributed over workers, so I think it would give us more power to handle retries and preemption in an iris layer rather than the DB layer. It also should delegate to Iris actors with a more lightweight interface than Ballista. I also like that it looks like this system will be integrated into DataFusion-Python soon: https://github.com/apache/datafusion-python/issues/1612. That said, the concerns that Will pointed out from the "when not to use this section" may be dealbreakers, and the right bet is to integrate Ballista into Iris workers. 

I also just posted in the DataFusion Discord to ask what the maintainers recommend. It might be that the best way to find out would be to build a small prototype with DataFusion.

## Responses to the above discussion

>  still doesn't mean you couldn't use the same distributed sql engine with scheduling similar to Zephyr's today for the larger data processing jobs.
> Why only share the shuffle? Presumably smallquery has would also need to do distributed maps for certain queries?
> there's no reason it couldn't also handle the things written in Python / Zephyr today.

I am 100% on this team; I think a SQL engine is the core thing you need for doing ELT/ETL, even for [non-tabular data](https://github.com/jayendra13/zarr-datafusion).

> How much of this could we reuse from Datafusion/Ballista? It looks like the main gap there would be the shuffles do temp writes to local disk. We could bring some of those ideas in though.

I agree, I think reusing DB technology is better than reinventing it, especially since distributed shuffles for reductions are non-trivial. I think DataFusion-Distributed would fit in the cleanest with Iris, if we can handle retry logic and persistence (maybe that makes Ballista the winner -- my original intention with https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/5861 was to have the DataFusion Context be swappable with a Ballista Context running on other workers in Iris). 

> ~100 sources, ~100k parquet files, ~35TB. In most cases we can assume parquet, but other formats would be nice to have.

35 TB is small. If we're looking for Marin Infra to support workloads in scientific applications like Coral, then we'd want to make sure this system scales to the 1s to 10s of petabytes IMO. We don't need to do this now, but it would be nice to know that such a thing is possible. (I still dream of loading all 12 PiBs of [ARCO-ERA5](https://github.com/google-research/arco-era5) into Marin). [Samudra](https://github.com/m2lines/Samudra), my primary project, is still looking for a core data engineering system replacement to Dask, and a 3 PiB dataset is on our roadmap to process.

> at some point I was curious if I could replace that with Arrow/Parquet, do you happen to have experience with that use-case? Scale ~20T. Actually, https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/4445 would be a good place to have this chat to keep this issue focused.

I'm part of the cult of [zarr.dev](https://zarr.dev), so I think Tensorstore on Zarr or maybe IceChunk is a better fit than parquet for Array shaped data. I think there could be a good opportunity to make a patch or extension to Orbax.

> I think it would probably look more like building sql support into Zephyr
> I'll work on a more coherent / detailed design proposal.

That's the dream. LMK if I can chat with you or collaborate on the design. I've done some work in this space.

comments.author: wmoss
claude[bot]
comments.body:
**Claude finished @wmoss's task in 2m 24s** —— [View job](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/actions/runs/28962455679)

---
### Ballista on Iris — deployment shape & failure model

I dug into how Zephyr deploys on Iris (the pattern you'd copy) and mapped Ballista's components onto it. TL;DR: deploying Ballista on Iris is mechanically easy and looks almost exactly like Zephyr's coordinator+workers; the hard part is exactly the one you flagged — **Ballista shuffles to executor-local disk, so an executor dying after it produced shuffle output forces recompute, and that recompute cascades under preemption.** Details below. I'd love @gabotechs to correct anything I get wrong about current Ballista internals.

---

### 1. The deployment is the easy part — it mirrors Zephyr almost 1:1

Zephyr already does the "scheduler + N executors per query" thing you're describing. One query = one Iris **job** that hosts the coordinator actor in-process and spins up an executor **actor group** as a child:

- `_run_coordinator_job` hosts the coordinator via `client.host_actor(...)` — [`execution.py:1543`](lib/zephyr/src/zephyr/execution.py#L1543)
- executors are a sized child actor group — `client.create_actor_group(ZephyrWorker, ..., count=actual_workers, resources=..., actor_config=ActorConfig(max_task_retries=10))` — [`execution.py:1571`](lib/zephyr/src/zephyr/execution.py#L1571)
- children are cascade-terminated when the coordinator job exits, so no orphaned executors ([`execution.py:6-11`](lib/zephyr/src/zephyr/execution.py#L4))

The Ballista analog:

| Ballista | Iris mapping |
|---|---|
| `ballista-scheduler` | one long-lived process — either the coordinator job itself, or a co-hosted actor (like Zephyr's in-process coordinator). Put it on the **non-preemptible** coordinator node from the design sketch above. |
| `ballista-executor` × N | a `create_actor_group(count=N)` of executor actors on preemptible workers, each running the executor gRPC server and registering with the scheduler |
| scheduler↔executor gRPC + Arrow Flight shuffle fetch | actor RPC endpoints; executors need to reach each other's Flight ports (Iris already gives every task a routable endpoint) |
| scheduler state store (in-mem / sled / etcd) | see §3 — this is where preemption survival is decided |

So "deploy scheduler + N executors per query" is a thin wrapper: a coordinator entrypoint that boots the scheduler, launches an executor actor group, submits the SQL, and writes results out. Nothing about Iris blocks this.

### 2. Executor failure — what actually happens

This is the crux. Ballista breaks the physical plan into **query stages** at every shuffle boundary. A `ShuffleWriterExec` at the end of a stage writes its output partitions as Arrow IPC files to the **executor's local disk**; the next stage's `ShuffleReaderExec` pulls those partitions from the producing executor over Arrow Flight.

Two distinct failure cases:

1. **Executor dies while running a task** → the scheduler sees the task fail / the executor heartbeat lapse, and reschedules that task onto another executor. This is fine — recompute one task from durable source data. Iris bringing up a replacement (the `max_task_retries` behavior) lines up with this; the new executor re-registers with the scheduler, just like Zephyr workers re-register after reconstruction ([`execution.py:351`](lib/zephyr/src/zephyr/execution.py#L351)).

2. **Executor dies *after* it finished a stage, and a downstream stage still needs its shuffle output** → that shuffle data was on local disk and is now **gone**. A reader hits a *fetch failure*. Ballista's recovery here is Spark-style: mark the lost shuffle partitions, and **re-run the map task(s) that produced them** (potentially the whole producing stage). Because the ultimate inputs are parquet in object storage, this is *recoverable in principle* — but under continuous preemption it **cascades**: re-running a producing stage means its executors write new shuffle files… which can also be lost before they're consumed. Query wall-time balloons; at enough scale/preemption rate the success probability collapses exactly as you predicted.

So the answer to "if an executor fails and Iris brings up another one, what happens?": the *running task* recovers cleanly, but any *already-materialized shuffle output on the dead node is lost and must be recomputed*, and that recompute is where preemption bites.

This is precisely why the design comment upthread proposes an **object-store shuffle with a per-attempt `_SUCCESS` committer** instead: once a stage's shuffle output is committed to GCS/CoreWeave, losing the executor costs you *nothing* — the durable partitions are still there, and a replacement executor just reads them. That's the property Zephyr already has (shuffle chunks live in the chunk store / object storage, not local disk), and it's the single most important thing Ballista does **not** give you out of the box.

### 3. Scheduler failure — does the whole query die?

Depends on the scheduler's state backend:

- **In-memory state (default single-scheduler)**: scheduler death = all job/stage/task state lost = **the query dies and cannot resume**. Restarting gives you a blank scheduler. This is the mode most people run.
- **Persistent state backend (sled embedded, or etcd in older versions)**: job graph and task/stage status are persisted, so a restarted scheduler can in principle recover in-flight jobs. In practice this path has historically been the less-exercised one, and it still doesn't rescue the lost *local-disk shuffle data* from §2 — it only rescues the *control-plane* state.

For Marin this means: keep the scheduler on the **non-preemptible** coordinator node (it's tiny — one per query), so scheduler loss is not a normal event. Then all the "can we survive preemption" weight lands on the executors, and the executor story only works if shuffle is durable (§2). Note this is a strictly *better* position than [datafusion-distributed's documented stance](https://datafusion-contrib.github.io/datafusion-distributed/index.html#when-not-to-use-this-library) ("any node fails → whole query fails; no retries; no intermediate persistence") — Ballista at least *has* task reschedule + shuffle-recompute, which is why @gabotechs is steering you to Ballista over datafusion-distributed for the preemption constraint.

### 4. Net assessment for the smallquery constraint

- **Deploying Ballista on Iris**: straightforward, copy the Zephyr coordinator/executor-group pattern.
- **Executor preemption**: survivable but *expensive* out-of-the-box because of local-disk shuffle → recompute cascade. The fix is durable (object-store) shuffle output — the same thing the design notes and @rjpower/@wmoss's "reusable shuffle lib" thread are circling.
- **Scheduler preemption**: pin the scheduler to the non-preemptible node; don't rely on Ballista HA state recovery for the common case.

Concretely, if you want to validate the failure math you asked for, the cheapest experiment is: run a single distributed join on Ballista-on-Iris, kill an executor **after** its shuffle-producing stage completes but **before** the consuming stage reads it, and measure (a) does it recover, (b) how much recompute it costs. That directly exercises the §2 case and tells you whether default Ballista is viable or whether the object-store-shuffle swap is mandatory before this is usable on preemptible capacity.

I kept this to analysis (no code changes) since the ask was to look into feasibility. Happy to prototype the coordinator/executor-group wrapper or the kill-an-executor test harness if you want to turn this into a spike.
 · branch `claude/issue-6761-20260708-1728`

comments.author: wmoss
comments.body:
Thanks @ravwojdyla, now I feel like I better understand what use cases we want to support.

@alxmrs I agree that DataFusion feels like the right solution here and I think Ballista is the only reasonable choice.

If we want to support long-running / large jobs, I think we need to use GCS for checkpointing stage output instead of local disk. Otherwise I think the intersection of long processing times, lots of workers and those workers getting preempted is going to kill job performance or worse, make it never finish.

I had Gemini do an analysis of having Ballista checkpoint to GCS (attached) and it was actually somewhat promising. The main things I was worried about was that Ballista would likely create a lot of small files from the shuffle, which it does out of the box, but it also supports a sort-based shuffle that writes one large file and has reducers seek into it (this is what Zephyr does). I'm less worried than Gemini about the cost of updating all the call sites to support object storage since I think AI's costing models are generally based on pre-AI costs. It also seems like something that we could, hopefully, commit back to Ballista, since I definitely don't want to be maintaining a long-running fork.

As a first PoC, my suggestion would actually be to use `gcsfuse` to mount a GCS bucket to the local filesystem. It will certainly be less performant than changing the Ballista code, but wouldn't actually require any code changes to Ballista to get something up and running just to see if it works. 

@alxmrs, I'm going to take over from Rav on the infra side here, but if you're stoked on this feel free to take a crack at it and I'm happy to collaborate. Otherwise I can point an AI at it and see how far it can get, but I've got plenty to keep me busy so you're welcome to run with it.

> One major technical note: SpiceAI already has a fork that we could adopt that would make Ballista work better for shuffles in our environment, see -- https://spice.ai/blog/apache-ballista-at-spice-ai

comments.author: wmoss
comments.body:
🤖 **Status update: Distributed DataFusion-Ballista PoC & Comparison on Iris**

We stood up a DataFusion-Ballista distributed scheduler and executor pool on-Iris and evaluated its performance against the standard Zephyr pipeline for the text normalization step. See the [draft PR #7588](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/7588) and the [detailed subissue #7266 comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7266#issuecomment-5065971169) for more information.

| Metric | Zephyr Pipeline | Ballista Pipeline (Optimized) | Speedup / Reduction |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Normalize Step Time** | **1h 20m 24s** (80.4 min) | **5m 33s** (5.5 min) | **14.4× faster** |
| **Overall Wall Time** | 1h 20m 47s | 5m 33s (non-concurrent mode) | **14.5× faster** |
| **GCS Scan / Read Count** | 1 pass (6 GB read) | 1 pass per query (288 GB total scanned) | ~48× increase (sequential planning) |
| **Output File Correctness** | 22 parquet shards | 22 parquet shards | Identical shard count & schemas |

---

### ⚠️ Critical Downsides & Limitations of Ballista

While the raw execution speed is a massive improvement, we identified severe developer and scalability limitations when compared to Zephyr:

1. **No Distributed Python UDFs**: Remote executors cannot deserialize and run Python objects. This meant we were *unable* to implement the existing Zephyr logic exactly; many things had to be changed to similar SQL patterns (e.g., native regexp/hash/string expressions). Expressing these complex transformations in SQL results in highly nested, verbose query strings that are difficult to read and make the control flow opaque.
2. **No native Gzip NdJson/CSV support (`json.gz`)**: Ballista remote executors cannot parse gzipped raw formats. This means we could not directly process existing Nemotron files without first decompressing or converting them.
3. **Query Planning & Scan Duplication (Sharding Overhead)**: Zephyr handles sharding in-memory in a single pass. Ballista requires planning and submitting $2 \times N_{shards}$ separate SQL queries concurrently. Because each query filters rows using a hash (e.g. `WHERE hash(id) % 22 = i`), executors must scan the raw dataset once per query. On a full-scale dataset (e.g., 4,136 shards), coordinating 8,272 queries would cause planning overhead and total scanned bytes to explode.

comments.author: ravwojdyla
comments.body: @wmoss nice!! The limitations make sense. I suspect in most cases we wouldn't want to implement full jobs using SQL, and in other cases we wouldn't be able to. We should consider if and how we would integrate it into our setup 🤞

comments.author: wmoss
comments.body:
My non-agent take is that getting it running was way easier than I thought. The agent had it up and running and computing `SELECT 1 + 1` and counting rows from GCS parquet files almost immediately. Then it got hung up for days (I wasn't being super active at poking it) trying to figure out how to actually mirror Zephyr functionality (and, as you can see, couldn't really do it in the end).

So I think overall I think,
- It would be great to augment ducky if queries get too big or too slow (I was running a 100 node cluster for these tests)
- It would probably work pretty well for data pipelines where you can express it easily in sql (although I didn't really test any of my concerns around long-running jobs)
- It doesn't seem like, at least without a fair amount of work, it can be a full replacement for Zephyr

Curious for your thoughts @ravwojdyla. You're much deeper in the data work than I am right now!

comments.author: ravwojdyla
wmoss
comments.body:
🤖 **Follow-up correction: Engine Per-Core Throughput & Concurrency Audit**

Following an audit of CPU time (`cpu_time_total`), the initial 14× wall-time difference was heavily confounded by worker count (Ballista ran on 80 workers while Zephyr auto-scaled to 5). 

Evaluating actual per-core compute throughput shows:
* **Zephyr (Python/PyArrow)**: **2.03 MB/s** per CPU core
* **Ballista (Rust/DataFusion)**: **11.07 MB/s** per CPU core

**Top-line correction**: On an apples-to-apples per-core basis, **Ballista's execution engine is ~5.5× faster than Zephyr**.

comments.author: claude[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 **Plan:**
- [x] Read AGENTS.md and skill playbooks
- [x] Check actionability (depends on #5995, several design choices unstated)
- [x] Survey existing zephyr skills and config surface
- [x] Post research + clarifying questions; no PR (design-sized, dep-blocked)

# Research

Two reasons this isn't PR-ready:

1. **Hard dep on #5995.** Bullet 2 ("use the stats from #5995") needs the `zephyr.stage` finelog stream from #5995, which isn't built yet — the proposed approach was just posted there today with open questions. A skill written against stats that don't exist will codify a fake schema. The skew-detection bullet has the same problem at per-shard granularity (`zephyr.shard`), and #5995's current scope explicitly defers per-shard rows.
2. **No definition of done for the skill itself.** The bullets describe *inputs to a heuristic*, not the skill's output, entry point, or scope. Concretely: where does the skill apply its recommendation (config file diff? new job submission? PR comment? chat reply?), what knobs does it touch (`map_workers_per_actor`, `reduce_workers_per_actor`, Iris `--memory`, scatter buffer fractions?), is it pre-job (plan from inputs only) or post-mortem (analyze a finished run) or mid-flight (suggest restart params)?

What's available today vs. what the skill would need:

| Need | Today | Gap |
|---|---|---|
| Shard count from inputs | [`readers.py#L98`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/zephyr/src/zephyr/readers.py#L98) `InputFileSpec`; row/byte ranges already supported | None — can list/size files via gsutil/fsspec |
| Per-stage throughput | [`execution.py#L191-L241`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/zephyr/src/zephyr/execution.py#L191-L241) `_stage_throughput` (in-process only) | Needs #5995 to land for cross-run history |
| Per-shard skew signal | [`OPS.md`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/zephyr/OPS.md) "Straggler Detection" — manual via `list-tasks` memoryMb + `actor call get_counters` | No durable per-shard counter stream (#5995 defers `zephyr.shard`) |
| Memory/thread knobs | [`execution.py#L1356`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/zephyr/src/zephyr/execution.py#L1356) `map_workers_per_actor` / `reduce_workers_per_actor`; Iris `--memory` on `job run` | None |

**Relevant code**
- [`readers.py#L98-L125`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/zephyr/src/zephyr/readers.py#L98-L125) — `InputFileSpec`, the natural shard unit
- [`execution.py#L1356-L1416`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/zephyr/src/zephyr/execution.py#L1356-L1416) — worker-slot knobs the skill would tune
- [`shuffle.py#L138-L142`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/zephyr/src/zephyr/shuffle.py#L138-L142) — scatter buffer is `memory / num_workers`, so memory and worker-count tune together
- [`OPS.md` — Straggler Detection / Data Skew](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/zephyr/OPS.md) — already documents the manual procedure a skill would automate
- [`.agents/skills/babysit-zephyr/SKILL.md`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/.agents/skills/babysit-zephyr/SKILL.md) and [`evaluate-zephyr-perf/SKILL.md`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/.agents/skills/evaluate-zephyr-perf/SKILL.md) — style/scope precedents (this skill is the missing third leg: pre-flight planner / post-mortem optimizer)

# Proposed approach (needs sign-off before writing the skill)

Split into two skills along the pre-job / post-job seam, since they use disjoint inputs and produce disjoint outputs:

**A. `plan-zephyr` (pre-job, no #5995 dep).** Input: a submission script or pipeline plan. Skill:
1. Resolves `InputFileSpec`s, enumerates files via fsspec, captures size and (for parquet) row counts.
2. Reports shard count and shard-size distribution (p50/p95/max/skew-ratio).
3. Picks `map_workers_per_actor`, `reduce_workers_per_actor`, and Iris `--memory` from a small heuristic table (e.g. memory = max(scatter-buffer-floor, p95 shard bytes × buffer-multiple); workers = min(cpu_count, p95-shard-mem-fit)).
4. Emits a diff against the user's submission command + a one-paragraph rationale. Does **not** auto-submit.

Doable now. ~100 LOC of skill prose + a small `scripts/zephyr/plan_inputs.py` helper for file enumeration (the heuristic itself stays in the skill prose; agents apply judgment).

**B. `tune-zephyr` (post-mortem, blocked on #5995).** Input: a finished or in-flight `iris_job_id`. Skill:
1. Pulls `zephyr.stage` rows for the run; flags stages where `item_rate` collapsed late (straggler signature) or `peak_worker_memory_mb` was close to allocation (under-provisioned).
2. Cross-references `iris.worker` (already exists) for OOM/preemption.
3. For skew, falls back to manual `actor call get_counters` per OPS.md until #5995 ships `zephyr.shard`.
4. Emits a recommended config delta for the next run, plus a "re-shard the input" recommendation when input skew is the dominant cost.

Out-of-scope for now (flag if you disagree):
- Auto-resubmitting with new params — risky without human review.
- Modifying scatter internals (covered by `evaluate-zephyr-perf`).
- CPU sizing — Iris already sets that per cluster config; not a Zephyr-side knob.

**Questions for @wmoss before I write either skill:**

- **(a) Split A/B or single skill?** I lean two skills (different inputs, different cadences, B blocks on #5995). Push back if you want one entry point.
- **(b) Output channel.** Print to terminal in the invoking chat (like `debug`), comment on a PR (like `evaluate-zephyr-perf`), or write a recommended config file? My default: terminal for A, comment on the issue/PR that owns the run for B.
- **(c) Heuristic provenance.** Do you have an existing rule-of-thumb for memory-per-shard / workers-per-actor I should encode, or should I derive defaults from a few representative ferries (datakit tier1/tier2/tier3) and bake those numbers in?
- **(d) Skew action.** When the skill flags skewed input shards, what's the recommended remediation in this codebase — a `repartition`/`reshuffle` op, manual `InputFileSpec` row-range splits, or just "tell the user and stop"?
- **(e) Defer B until #5995 lands?** Or stub it now against the proposed schema and update when #5995 lands?

Holding off on PRs pending answers, since (b)–(d) materially change the skill's content.

spillover_issues.body:
## Full Qwen panel, November 20

**102 tasks inventoried; 101 planned per knowledge condition (202 Qwen trials).** Task 78 covers mutation-specific protein stability prediction and includes a toxin in its held-out examples. Its inventory entry is retained, with both knowledge conditions marked unrun and no score assigned. Report coverage against the official 102-task inventory. Once all eligible tasks are graded, each headline score has a denominator of 101. EvalDash submitted both conditions on November 20 at 16:15 UTC. The first 13 knowledge-on grades were verified in the official archive, each with positive Qwen completion tokens. Knowledge-off had 29 admitted trials and zero grades after an infrastructure interruption. Its three unused judge reservations were reconciled against a complete sandbox audit, with zero visual grader launches in the interruption window. The knowledge-off retry will reuse the original run identity and budget. [Submitted runs](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11592#issuecomment-7044520121) The earlier 204-trial preflight and the single-task pilot are historical checkpoints. [Implementation PR](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11599)

**Task 41 stays in both conditions at the released threshold of 0.73.** Flag its reference failure beside the headline results and also report each condition’s aggregate with task 41 excluded. Anika Liu and coauthors supplied the underlying study. The ScienceAgentBench team published the KNN adaptation, reference program and grader. We measured mean F1 of 0.70433 for the released reference on the released inputs with scikit-learn 1.7.2, 1.5.2 and 1.4.2. Each replay earned zero. The origin of the published threshold remains unresolved. [Original study code](https://github.com/anikaliu/CAMDA-DILI/blob/master/Machine_Learning/code/models_MD.py) · [ScienceAgentBench Verified release](https://github.com/OSU-NLP-Group/ScienceAgentBench#updates)

**Visual reference failures stay in the headline results.** Use the published task thresholds and missing-marker rule in both knowledge conditions. Task 59’s publisher plot averaged 0 (all three replies hit the output limit without a score marker). Task 96’s averaged 36.67. Both have a threshold of 60. Freeze the list of reference failures before inspecting Qwen outcomes. For each condition report the headline score and denominator, the task-41-only exclusion, and the score and denominator after excluding all flagged reference failures. List each excluded ID and its reason. Track incomplete reference checks and infrastructure failures separately.

### Publisher reference results for the 101 eligible tasks

| Outcome | Tasks | Interpretation |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| Passed a deterministic evaluator | 29 | Task 97 used an extended diagnostic allowance. Its pass within the official 900-second clean replay limit is unverified. |
| Passed visual grading | 58 | The last recovered plot, task 52, averaged 73 against a threshold of 60. |
| Produced an output below the published threshold | 4 | Tasks 41, 59, 96 and 102. These four define the threshold-failure sensitivity analysis. |
| No completed output comparison | 10 | Tasks 11, 12, 13, 15, 70, 72, 75 and 90 encountered replay failures or timeouts. Task 17's publisher program required Kaleido for plot export. Task 49's judge request was interrupted. |

The four groups count each eligible task once. The visual ledger has 61 completed figure comparisons for 60 tasks because task 63 has two figures. The reference flags were frozen before Qwen inference began. Tasks 53 and 58 have a separate sensitivity analysis for answer exposure. [Reference results and thresholds](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11592#issuecomment-7045716068)

## Task 66 pilot result, November 19

**Qwen received 0/1 on task 66 with expert knowledge off.** The official EvalDash run used Pi 0.87.0 with a 65,536-token context and a 16,384-token reply cap. A fresh sandbox staged the task CSV after startup from the pinned release. The submitted program exited successfully in clean replay. Three independent MiniMax M3 comparisons scored its plot 45, 30 and 55. Their mean of 43.33 fell below the published threshold of 60. The judge calls cost $0.00314458. [Official shared-image run](https://marina.oa.dev/evaldash/runs/20261119-194500-qwen3.6-35b-a3b-9d050394062043259c60bdafbc0db1dd-scienceagentbench-verified-66-knowledge-off-08d3fc592fd85680ac9670b7ab000efe)

An earlier integration run on the same case also received 0/1. It used an image containing the CSV. Its three scores were 45, 0 and 35. One completion hit its output limit without a score marker and received zero under the published rule. The matched and mismatched plot controls averaged 96 and 25. Both runs used OpenRouter with DeepInfra FP8 and fallback disabled. Equivalence to the self-hosted MXFP8 checkpoint remains unverified. [Earlier integration run](https://iris.oa.dev/#/job/%2Fexedev%2Fsab66-official-openrouter-1119e)

| Evidence | November 19 checkpoint |
| --- | --- |
| Official Qwen pilot | One distinct knowledge-off case, reward 0, on the earlier 1 GiB allocation |
| Full Qwen cohort panel | 204 cases prepared on 2 CPUs, 8 GiB RAM and 10 GiB disk. Zero solver starts and zero grades |
| Publisher reference controls | 73 of 102 task IDs exercised across shared-image revisions. Nineteen distinct deterministic references passed. Visual output checks and judge verdicts are recorded separately |
| Visual-judge budget | Up to 390 candidate calls for both conditions. Up to 195 additional reference-control calls were approved under the same aggregate $5 ceiling |

## Summary

Implement [ScienceAgentBench Verified](https://github.com/OSU-NLP-Group/ScienceAgentBench)
with Pi through the native TaskSpec and EvalDash route and collect evidence for inclusion in
[Marin's ID evaluation policy](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10197).
The proposed outcome is a reproducible implementation, complete runs on selected
cohort models through the official EvalDash path, and a documented admission
recommendation. Policy inclusion remains a separate decision.

Execution order: implement and validate the 101 eligible reference solutions, run the
202-trial Qwen panel through the official evaluation path, review its outcomes,
run the remaining cohort, and present the admission recommendation.

The task 66 pilot exercised the native agentic path end to end. The remaining admission evidence depends on validating the publisher references and running the cohort. Harbor’s existing adapter provides the comparison for the original release.

The benchmark tests scientific Python programming with supplied data across
bioinformatics, computational chemistry, geographical information science, and
psychology/cognitive science. The inclusion case will document the measured
capabilities, trustworthy grading, cohort results, reproducibility, and
operational cost. An incremental-coverage or overlap assessment against existing
ID evaluations is outside this issue's scope.

## Evidence standard

[SimpleQA Verified PR #11393](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11393)
provides an example of the evidence package for a new evaluation:

- What capability is measured and why it belongs in the evaluation set.
- Pinned data, implementation, prompts, models, and explicit protocol deviations.
- Complete baseline runs with EvalDash links and comparison to published results.
- Grading audits, failures, and limitations.
- End-to-end runtime, accelerator use, and judge cost.

Registration, full execution, verified dashboard ingestion, and policy admission
are separate milestones. An EvalDash entry alone does not establish policy approval.

## Source findings

### Verified modifies the original task population

It is a modification of the same 102 task IDs, not a smaller subset.

<details>
<summary>Annotation comparison: 41 of 102 rows changed</summary>

A direct comparison of the public annotation files at Hugging Face revision
`9c6e96c9e74572e979b0930ee735041cef528cb7` found:

| Comparison | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Original annotation rows | 102 |
| Verified annotation rows | 102 |
| Added or removed instance IDs | None |
| Rows with at least one changed field | 41 |
| Task instruction changes | 9 tasks |
| Domain knowledge changes | 4 tasks |
| Dataset preview changes | 18 tasks |
| Source file/path changes | 15 tasks |

Field counts overlap. The comparison normalized null and empty values to the same
empty string and compared other values as strings; it is an annotation comparison,
not an audit of the underlying datasets or grading artifacts.

Changed task instructions: 12, 26, 29, 31, 32, 34, 35, 67, 92.
Changed domain knowledge: 5, 9, 79, 80.

Sources:
[original CSV](https://huggingface.co/datasets/osunlp/ScienceAgentBench/blob/9c6e96c9e74572e979b0930ee735041cef528cb7/ScienceAgentBench.csv),
[Verified annotations](https://huggingface.co/datasets/osunlp/ScienceAgentBench/blob/9c6e96c9e74572e979b0930ee735041cef528cb7/data/verified-00000-of-00001.parquet).

</details>

Upstream describes Verified as a release to reduce false negatives and requires
both the Verified annotations and `benchmark_verified.zip`. The November 17
artifact audit below establishes its inventory and selected grading structure.
The historical artifact link returns HTTP 404, so exact legacy-to-Verified
evaluator, reference-output, input-data, and dependency changes remain unresolved.
Do not describe this as a grading-only fix.

### Verified artifact audit — November 17, 2026

The archive linked by the current upstream README is 1,769,478,786 bytes;
streamed SHA-256: `46e715d3b2196d459d2dff52aa487f506a95ec44b44262e82208d086ea879610`.
Its 955 entries total 4,071,815,117 uncompressed bytes. Ranged reads retrieved
only the small program/rubric files for static inspection; restricted source
files remain private and were not committed or redistributed.

- All 102 annotation-referenced evaluators and reference programs are present.
  There are 110 Python files in the evaluator directory; only the annotation
  mapping defines the evaluation population.
- The selected evaluators comprise 38 deterministic and 64 visual tasks.
  Sixty-three visual tasks make one figure comparison. Task 63 makes two;
  each figure's mean judge score must be at least 60 for the task to pass.
  The single-figure visual evaluators also use the threshold of 60.
- Task 63 requires both figure outputs. Capturing only each annotation's
  `output_fname` would omit its second output; capture the required output set
  from clean replay before grading.
- Task 22 calls `pandas.read_pickle` on candidate output. Its deserialization
  requires an additional isolation boundary or an explicitly validated safe
  representation; moving program execution out of the grader is insufficient
  to isolate that task's untrusted output.
- The largest dataset directory is approximately 863.28 MiB. This is input-data
  size, not prepared image size or peak disk usage, and does not yet prove that
  every task fits the selected 10 GiB allocation.

This audit is static evidence. Reference execution, full data/dependency
validation, and the original-versus-Verified artifact comparison remain pending.

### Harbor generation is unpinned and targets the legacy split

There are two separate issues:

1. **Reproducibility:** the generator calls `load_dataset` without a revision.
   Regenerating tasks can therefore change when upstream changes. This is a
   reproducibility defect for a canonical evaluation, though it does not prove
   already-generated, separately pinned Harbor tasks are mutable.
2. **Current loader compatibility:** the generator loads the default configuration
   and indexes `['validation']`. The current HF default configuration exposes
   `verified`; the legacy `validation` split lives in a separate configuration
   named `validation`. The existing code is therefore expected to fail on a fresh
   current load with a missing-split error. This is a source-level finding; the
   adapter has not been executed here.

For Verified, explicitly select `split="verified"` and a full HF revision, paired
with the matching artifact checksum. Reproducing the legacy benchmark requires an
explicit legacy config/revision and its matching artifacts. Neither choice should
silently replace the other.

Sources: [adapter.py](https://github.com/harbor-framework/harbor/blob/e5a08396fce7bc230b2f023bbb568dbfa86b3ee8/adapters/scienceagentbench/adapter.py),
[run_adapter.py](https://github.com/harbor-framework/harbor/blob/e5a08396fce7bc230b2f023bbb568dbfa86b3ee8/adapters/scienceagentbench/run_adapter.py),
[HF configuration](https://huggingface.co/datasets/osunlp/ScienceAgentBench/blob/9c6e96c9e74572e979b0930ee735041cef528cb7/README.md).

## Existing implementation and evidence

- [Harbor PR #630](https://github.com/harbor-framework/harbor/pull/630) merged on
  April 18, 2026. [Upstream](https://github.com/OSU-NLP-Group/ScienceAgentBench)
  announced Verified on April 30, 2026.
- Harbor documents 102 legacy tasks: 38 deterministic and 64 visual-judge tasks.
  Recheck this classification against Verified artifacts.
- Historical parity used Claude Code 2.1.63 with Claude Haiku 4.5, five runs per
  framework: Harbor 31.76% ± 1.18 percentage points SEM; patched upstream harness
  33.72% ± 0.91. The upstream harness had output-path and dependency fixes. These
  are legacy parity results, not Verified or Marin results.
- The current README reports 95/102 CPU oracle passes, with failures attributed
  to resource needs and stochastic variation. The PR description reports 100/102;
  that discrepancy needs reconciliation rather than selecting the stronger claim.
- Earlier Marin research in [issue #9160](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9160)
  prioritized a deterministic bioinformatics subset for readiness checks. That is
  a different scope from full Verified evaluation.

## Grading concerns to resolve

The [Harbor verifier](https://github.com/harbor-framework/harbor/blob/e5a08396fce7bc230b2f023bbb568dbfa86b3ee8/adapters/scienceagentbench/template/tests/test.sh)
turns missing or unreadable evaluation results into zero rewards. Infrastructure
failures must remain distinguishable from valid model failures.

The verifier also copies gold references into the execution filesystem before
rerunning submitted code. Although they are hidden during agent generation, they
are accessible during that later execution. Separate submitted-program execution
from grading, including reference files and judge credentials. This is a static
boundary finding, not an observed exploitation result.

The upstream visual judge uses GPT-4o-2024-05-13, temperature 0.2, top-p 0.95, 1,000 output
tokens, and three completions per request (`n=3`). Missing score markers become
zero in both inspected upstream and Harbor implementations. Decide and document
whether to preserve that behavior for parity or use an explicitly versioned
failure-aware protocol. Do not silently change grading semantics. Extract, pin, and test Verified's
exact task-success calculation, including aggregation across multiple figures
and mixed checks, pass thresholds, and missing candidate-output rules. Keep
malformed judge responses separate from valid negative judgments.

Sources: [upstream judge](https://github.com/OSU-NLP-Group/ScienceAgentBench/blob/c26e151ed601ba109dc4d35e057ff8e73fec469d/gpt4_visual_judge.py),
[Harbor judge](https://github.com/harbor-framework/harbor/blob/e5a08396fce7bc230b2f023bbb568dbfa86b3ee8/adapters/scienceagentbench/llm_visual_judge.py).

## Execution route

The development pilot ran through the official EvalDash launcher with TaskSpec, Pi 0.87.0, and Daytona. TaskSpec describes the task, files, environment and grader. Pi runs the interactive coding session. A fresh sandbox replays the submitted program, then a separate grader receives its outputs and the publisher’s grading material. The shared-image task 66 record shows this path working end to end.

The initial plan followed BixBench’s Harbor adapter because the new-eval guide at the time covered non-agentic tasks. Harbor remains the comparison for the legacy ScienceAgentBench release, and BixBench provides the Pi and cohort settings. The native route now has a graded pilot in EvalDash. [Implementation PR](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11599) · [Historical non-agentic guide](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/2dd5aa45254641ef3c2977afa49cdc2afa34c1e6/docs/tutorials/add-evaluation.md)

Upstream's [metric calculation](https://github.com/OSU-NLP-Group/ScienceAgentBench/blob/c26e151ed601ba109dc4d35e057ff8e73fec469d/calculate_metrics.py)
selects the best trajectory separately for each task, using success, program
validity, CodeBERTScore, then cost to break ties. Its reported cost averages the
selected trajectories. Our operational cost report must count all attempts,
retries, and judge calls, including trajectories that were not selected.

The official [inference instructions](https://github.com/OSU-NLP-Group/ScienceAgentBench/blob/c26e151ed601ba109dc4d35e057ff8e73fec469d/README.md#direct-prompting-and-self-debug)
expose `--use_knowledge` as an option, and the
[native agent](https://github.com/OSU-NLP-Group/ScienceAgentBench/blob/c26e151ed601ba109dc4d35e057ff8e73fec469d/agent.py)
defaults to `use_knowledge=False`. Including the supplied knowledge is a supported
benchmark variant. Here the repository agent means the authors' direct-prompting
and self-debug implementation, not a uniquely canonical agent protocol.
[Paper Table 3](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.05080v3#S4.T3) reports both with-knowledge
and without-knowledge results for direct prompting, OpenHands CodeAct, and
self-debug. The code default does not establish a preferred paper setting.
These paper results predate Verified. Comparisons must match the knowledge
setting as well as the benchmark version. The selected plan is two separately
reported conditions for each of the three models: six model-condition cells.
One trial per task per model per knowledge condition is selected: 612 planned
solver trials, excluding validation and separately accounted infrastructure
retries. This protocol decision does not authorize execution or spending.

### Image preparation strategy (selected)

Selected: prepare and validate images before scored trials, then use immutable image digests
across models, knowledge conditions, and retries. This is compatible with the
TaskSpec image route, which requires resolving Docker build recipes before
execution. A fresh container per trial still preserves isolation; reusing an image
must never reuse a model's modified workspace.

BixBench and BFCL campaign configurations explicitly require preparing selected
task images with Pi before launch. Policy #10197 describes DS-1000 images built
from pinned Dockerfiles; that statement does not establish whether builds occur
for every trial or whether caches are reused. There is no single image-preparation
procedure established here for every policy evaluation.

A completed November 5 BixBench Pi run provides a narrower historical check:
its saved job configuration and 205-trial lock select the pinned Dockerfile-based
task repository, without a prepared-image override. A sampled trial completed
grading without an infrastructure exception. Those artifacts do not identify a
final prepared-image registry or digest, so they do not establish that the
current campaign's preparation requirement was followed in that run.

SAB's Harbor adapter provides Dockerfile recipes with scientific dependencies and
task input data. Those recipes can be built ahead of time. For the proposed
Verified implementation, invoke Pi only during the actor stage, keep clean replay
free of gold references and judge credentials, and expose private grading assets
only to the grading stage. Actor and replay use the same prepared scientific
environment; the replay stage runs the submitted Python program directly.

The pinned upstream container harness builds task dependencies from imports in
the submitted program using `pipreqs`, followed by task-specific installation
rules. It uses Python 3.10 and several version ranges rather than a complete lock.
That harness was released after the paper; it is not evidence of the paper's exact
environment. Fixed prepared images therefore change dependency provisioning.
Record the resolved package lock, system dependencies, base-image digests and recipe identity. Validate every reference program before scored use.

The shared software recipe pins the runtime across both knowledge conditions. Each fresh sandbox receives only the files for its task. Record disk use and staging time independently of solver time. A changed dependency requires a new recipe version and reference validation.

The image-build deadline governs preparation work, separately from the six-minute
agent setup, 60-minute solving, and 30-minute verifier budgets. Match BixBench's
preparation behavior without a benchmark-specific timeout override. Verify and
record the effective timeout in the preparation path before building; no explicit
campaign override does not imply unlimited build time. Harbor's 30-minute SAB
template allowance is comparison evidence, not the selected preparation limit.

### Timing evidence for the protocol decision

The [paper introduction](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.05080v3#S1) says agents can
usually produce a meaningful program draft within 10 minutes. This is a broad
observation, not a reported end-to-end runtime distribution or agent deadline.
[Appendix A](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.05080v3#A1) says task collection was
restricted to programs that complete within 10 minutes; this concerns program
execution, not the entire agent session.

In upstream code at `c26e151ed601ba109dc4d35e057ff8e73fec469d`,
[agent.py](https://github.com/OSU-NLP-Group/ScienceAgentBench/blob/c26e151ed601ba109dc4d35e057ff8e73fec469d/agent.py)
allows up to 10 self-debug iterations and 900 seconds per program execution.
[run_eval.py](https://github.com/OSU-NLP-Group/ScienceAgentBench/blob/c26e151ed601ba109dc4d35e057ff8e73fec469d/run_eval.py)
also uses 900 seconds for submitted-program execution. The
[Docker evaluation CLI](https://github.com/OSU-NLP-Group/ScienceAgentBench/blob/c26e151ed601ba109dc4d35e057ff8e73fec469d/evaluation/harness/run_evaluation.py)
defaults to 1,800 seconds for tests per instance. These are distinct limits.
The selected Pi agent budget is 60 minutes per task, matching the Harbor adapter
default. The selected verifier budget is 30 minutes total, including clean
execution capped at 900 seconds. These are Marin protocol choices, not
paper-specified agent deadlines.

runtime readiness or policy approval; the validation gates still apply.

| Official Verified release, preserving all 102 task IDs | Reuse the legacy Harbor dataset unchanged | Verified includes upstream corrections. It requires auditing updated artifacts and graders; legacy Harbor results remain historical comparisons, not Verified evidence. |
| Retain and flag the exposed answers in tasks 53 and 58 | Remove the three matching files for those tasks only | Keeping the published inputs preserves comparability. Removing them would create a corrected-input variant. |

A Harbor-only update could reuse more existing wiring, while TaskSpec plus Pi requires proving the shared runner integration. ShellHarness would change the selected agent. |

It exposes more compute to integration failures, so full reference validation precedes it. |
